title: Trump Repeats a Centuries-Old Mistake
excerpt: This is a special Election Day edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is a special Election Day edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present

Sign up here. “The President of the United States has so singular a combination of defects for the office of a constitutional magistrate, that he could have obtained the opportunity to misrule the nation only by a visitation of Providence.” So begins one of the most withering paragraphs on politics in the history of The Atlantic . “He unites in his character the seemingly opposite qualities of demagogue and autocrat,” the passage continues, “and converts the Presidential chair into a stump or a throne, according as the impulse seizes him to cajole or to command.” These words, written by E
Whipple , date back to September 1866, in the midst of a midterm election battle
The sitting president, Andrew Johnson, had been thrust into office a little more than a year earlier by John Wilkes Booth
By the time Whipple’s essay appeared, Johnson had placed himself at the center of a congressional election that would have defining consequences for the country
With the guns of the Civil War still warm, the fundamental questions of Reconstruction were at the core of national politics

The Republican majority in Congress insisted that Reconstruction must do more than simply restore Confederate states to the Union: It must secure the rights of formerly enslaved people and prevent certain former Confederate leaders from returning to political power
Johnson, a War Democrat from Tennessee who’d been nominated to balance Abraham Lincoln’s National Union ticket in 1864, took another view
Whipple’s essays on the theatrics of Johnson’s campaign are the work of a writer at the height of his powers, but who also may be losing his mind
Whipple performed surgical eviscerations of Johnson and his allies’ efforts to nullify the Union triumph in the Civil War

Nearly blinded by his racism and opposition to Black civil rights, Johnson set himself at odds with the Republican majority, pardoning thousands of former Confederates, vetoing Reconstruction legislation, and excusing white violence on Black Americans in Memphis and New Orleans

In his essays, Whipple confronted the maddening diversions of what he called the “Johnson Party,” in which secessionists were portrayed as the true patriots, presidential overreach and usurpation were said to be in service of the Constitution, and those opposing both were seen as the real traitors. “There is no wrong anywhere,” Whipple lamented. “It is all ‘right.’” Whipple’s shouts resonate in our own up-is-down era of politics, and in a midterm cycle in which Donald Trump, like Johnson in 1866, “sees hardly anything as it is, but almost everything as colored by his own dominant egotism.” Trump’s attempt to hold on to his party’s majority has focused on defending his record and deflecting questions about affordability and high gas prices

Some Republican candidates are distancing themselves from him ahead of Election Day, as his appearances veer into unusual tangents removed from voters’ everyday concerns (for good measure, he recently took to praising the “ass” of Senator Jon Husted of Ohio and the rapper Nicki Minaj )
Johnson, too, defined the election as a referendum not just on the nation and its future, but on his destiny in shaping it
With whispers of a possible impeachment dogging him that year, the midterms represented a showdown between the executive and legislative branches

Whipple’s essay on “The Johnson Party” came after the so-called National Union Convention, an August 1866 event that Johnson and his Cabinet had endorsed to form a new coalition that could displace the pro-Reconstruction Republican majority in Congress
In the case that Johnson’s new party failed to win, some of his supporters reportedly discussed schemes to deny Republicans power

If “Congress cannot be overcome by fair means, it will be by foul,” Whipple wrote. “In short, we are promised, on the assembling of the next Congress, a coup d’état .” To rally support for his Reconstruction policies and preferred congressional candidates, Johnson embarked on an unsuccessful national tour. (Whipple argued that he did so “with the intention of carrying the country by assault.”) His endeavors wound up hurting, rather than helping, his cause
He took to the stump to advocate for his own interests, with Whipple noting “the immense protuberance” of the first-person pronoun throughout the president’s many speeches
Although he didn’t make the posteriors of his political allies central to his closing argument, in the end, he was deemed a “Presidential Ass” by a Michigan Republican
Such presidential barnstorming amid a congressional election was something of a novelty that many deemed beneath the dignity of the office; the intemperate content of Johnson’s speeches made it worse
His remarks at times devolved into “a volcanic outbreak of vulgarity, conceit, bombast, scurrility, ignorance, insolence, brutality, and balderdash,” according to Whipple
When Johnson found himself assailed by hecklers (who he claimed were paid disrupters), his material took dark and strange turns

After one audience member called for the hanging of the Confederate president, Jefferson Davis, Johnson in turn suggested hanging the Republican representative Thaddeus Stevens and the abolitionist Wendell Phillips
Subsequent jeers inspired him to compare himself to Christ, betrayed by Judas and suffering on behalf of the nation at large
Governors, mayors, and other politicians were reportedly avoiding the president’s appearances, sometimes declining to welcome him or leaving town before he arrived
As the tour concluded in the middle of September, the magnitude of Johnson’s mistake came into view
By one senator’s estimate, Johnson’s campaigning cost his preferred candidates roughly a million votes across the country—no small number in that era’s electorate
The New York Times reportedly lost nearly a third of its mostly Republican subscribers after its editor, Henry Jarvis Raymond, had openly supported Johnson and the National Union movement

Most important, the very Republicans whom Johnson had wished to displace didn’t lose seats but gained them, beyond the two-thirds majority necessary to override the presidential veto that Johnson had already used against Reconstruction legislation
And Johnson, for his part, later became the first president to ever be impeached
The 1866 midterms took place in an entirely different world from ours
A president campaigning on behalf of congressional candidates was uncommon then, and a president routinely violating the decorum and propriety associated with the office was more uncommon yet
Whipple hoped that voters would go on to “indignantly record the most overwhelming of verdicts” against Johnson
Now, 160 years later, America once more has a president who has elevated his own ambitions above the nation’s

title: Six Books You Should Read Twice
excerpt: In the seven years I taught writing to first-year university students, I always began the semester the same way: We’d start with lessons on how to read critical
body: In the seven years I taught writing to first-year university students, I always began the semester the same way: We’d start with lessons on how to read critically
To help them, I introduced the concept of the hermeneutic circle—a fancy philosophical name for a simple idea
To comprehend the meaning of a book, readers need to analyze its individual sentences and paragraphs, but those parts can’t be interpreted without understanding how they work as a whole
In practice, this usually means reading to the end and going right back to the beginning
The hermeneutic circle isn’t just for academics, though; it explains why some novels feel impossible to put down
You’re using it when you flip back to the opening of a mystery after you’ve reached a pivotal scene that changes what you thought you knew
Sometimes a plot twist completely flips your understanding of a character, and you can’t help but reread the novel, this time with your eyes wide open
The six books below feature unreliable narrators, jarring perspective shifts, and slow-burning reveals
As soon as they’re over, they demand to be instantly started again
Devil House , by John Darnielle Darnielle, the front man for the indie band the Mountain Goats, starts his third novel simply enough
Gage Chandler, a once-acclaimed true-crime writer, is sniffing out what just might be his next hit: an investigation into a 1986 unsolved double murder at a former porn shop
Some 20 years later, Chandler has moved into the scene of the crime, dubbed “Devil House,” to immerse himself in the story
But the more time he spends going through grisly source material purchased from eBay, the more he chafes at his task

Then Darnielle takes Devil House down a series of sharp left turns, and each new section feels like its own book: This meta-novel grows to include the story of the crime that inspired Chandler’s debut, The White Witch of Morro Bay , and a faux–Middle English myth rendered in Gothic font
Darnielle’s eventual return to Devil House—and Chandler’s accounting of the costs of digging up its history—is no less surprising

The reader is left to reassemble this dissection of the true-crime genre, and then to ponder what it means to arrange jumbled puzzle pieces into a coherent portrait. [ Read: 15 books you won’t regret rereading ] Dirtbag, Massachusetts , by Isaac Fitzgerald Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional , and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing

The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13
But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life
As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive

Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead , by Olga Tokarczuk, trans lated by Antonia Lloyd-Jones Janina Duszejko, the strange older woman who narrates this Nobel Laureate’s fairy tale–tinged noir thriller, seems too caught up in her devotion to animals, astrology, and the poetry of William Blake to involve herself in anything as petty as a whodunit

But when poachers start turning up dead in Duszejko’s remote Polish hamlet in the Kłodzko Valley, she fights to make the police listen to her theory of the crimes: The animals who have long made their home in the village’s bordering forest are taking their revenge

In Tokarczuk’s hands, Duszejko is no “crazy madwoman,” as the police see her, but a prophet—the only one who can see that “animals have a very strong sense of justice.” On a second pass, with full knowledge of why Duszejko becomes so wrapped up in the murder investigations, you can better appreciate how Tokarczuk subverts the thriller’s typical form with a philosophical meditation on how humans have become all too comfortable with destroying the natural world. [ Read: The case for rereading the high-school classics ] Loved and Missed , by Susie Boyt I picked up Loved and Missed after seeing it recommended again and again by fellow critics as a touching, engrossing novel about the pleasures of caregiving , one that they were desperate to talk about

The book—largely narrated by a middle-aged schoolteacher named Ruth as she takes over the parenting of her granddaughter, Lily, from her drug-addicted daughter, Eleanor—is indeed poignant and charming

Ruth builds a cozy home life after deciding that Lily “was not going to have a poultice childhood, a mending service, scrappy and provisional.” Yet buzzing beneath this domestic bliss is the live wire of Eleanor’s presence and absence, and the reader is forced to wonder how Lily is affected by being the object of all of Ruth’s displaced motherly love
Then, in the last chapter, Boyt hands the reins of narration to the teenage Lily, adding a fresh charge to all that came before

She’s Under Here: A Love Story, a Horror Story, a Reckoning , by Karen Palmer The first time I read Palmer’s memoir of fleeing her abusive ex-husband and assuming a new identity, I hardly came up for air

I was fully submerged in her recounting of 14 dangerous years of marriage—including a harrowing scene of her ex holding a gun to her pregnant belly—followed by escalating torment after she flees with her daughters

But this memoir of surviving domestic violence and then coming to terms with what it costs to start over entirely, including forged birth certificates and a fake life story, deserves to be lingered over, just as Palmer’s fear stayed with her for decades

Only on my second read, once I had made it through with Palmer to safer shores, was I able to fully appreciate the author’s persistent doubts about the choices she was forced to make, as well her haunting meditations on why she stayed for so long. [ Read: What rereading childhood books teaches adults about themselves ] Women and Children First , by Alina Grabowski The fictional decaying coastal town of Nashquitten, Massachusetts, is a place where “it seemed like there was a death every month”—opioid overdoses, drunk driving, suicides
But the mysterious death of the aspiring artist Lucy Anderson at a high-school party stands out

Grabowski follows the ripples and rifts that led to and came after Lucy’s demise via a Rashomon -like structure, switching among the perspectives of 10 different girls and women connected to Lucy: her classmate, her guidance counselor, her best friend, her mother
Each narrator’s story offers a shard of what happened at that party, yet their points of view are contradictory and hopelessly biased, each coloring the reader’s understanding of what came before
Women and Children First is less a puzzle than a kaleidoscope, offering several misaligned but interconnected visions of the truth

The satisfaction comes not from any definitive reveal of what happened to Lucy, but from unraveling how all these characters’ actions and stories affect one another—something you can only really understand once you’ve finished the book and gone back to page one.

title: Three Tips for Watching the Results Roll In
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
I have a confession to make: As a political journalist, I hate Election Day
It’s a day when it’s too late to report or write anything that will inform readers or illuminate the campaign, but it’s also too soon to have the results and analyze them
That leaves me with nothing but nervous energy and nowhere to channel it

Perhaps you feel some of this anxiety too—especially given how high-stakes elections feel for Americans of all political views. ( Stat News reported last week that hospitals see more heart-attack cases right after Election Day.) Having a plan for how to absorb the news this evening is one way to soothe your nerves
Leave the Magic Walls, Big Boards, and comprehensive tracking of House races to John King and Steve Kornacki
You don’t need to worry about what’s going on in, say, Florida’s Twenty-Seventh District with 17 percent of the vote counted
The first polls close at 6 p.m. eastern today, but many of the states with pivotal elections won’t stop voting until 8 or 9 p.m. eastern; Alaskan polling locations close at 1 a.m. eastern
Pick just a few races that are of particular interest to you—either because you live somewhere with a contested race or because you’re especially interested in some candidate
You can also stay focused on the big ideas and stakes by watching The Atlantic ’s livestream, featuring Tom Nichols, David Frum, Anne Applebaum, and more
That starts at 9 p.m. eastern on TheAtlantic.com and on our app

Several races might be good indicators of where the rest of the election is headed. (I hope needless to say, but don’t pay attention to the early exit polls , whatever you do.) The first of the major Senate polls to close will be at 7:30 in Ohio, where the GOP incumbent Jon Husted—he of the supposedly callipygian physique —is facing off against the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown

Maine and most of Michigan, also pivotal Senate races, close at 8, though Democratic hopes will ride on turnout in Detroit, where vote counting was very slow in 2020 and 2024, so don’t bet on an early call there
In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas is favored over Republican John Sununu, but if the result is close, it might be a reason for Democrats to temper hopes

The same is true in Minnesota, where Democrat Peggy Flanagan is expected to hold off Republican Michele Tafoya. (If either Democrat loses, expect panic left of center.) In South Carolina, the short-term Republican incumbent, Darline Graham, seems to have the edge—major forecasters rate the race as leaning Republican—but if Democrat Annie Andrews is close, that would suggest strong Democratic results elsewhere. (If Andrews wins, it will be Republicans panicking.) Second, remember that there’s no such thing as a final result on Election Night
Unfortunately, reporters and anchors tend to discuss results coming in from local officials as though the votes are being cast in real time, saying that a candidate is “pulling ahead” and the like
Race calls from networks or the Associated Press are merely judgments about who will win, not binding in any way
In fact, races are complete only when officials certify them, and the order in which votes are counted is irrelevant to the outcome

This is especially important because of a phenomenon known as the “ blue shift ”: For a variety of reasons, including the prevalence of Democratic voters in urban centers that have more votes and count more slowly, Democratic votes tend to be fully tallied later
The result is that an election that looks more favorable to Republicans based on early returns may turn out to be less so
Although President Trump has claimed blue shifts are evidence of fraud, this is not true
The idea that no outcome is valid until all votes are counted might seem intuitive, but it is lost even on some members of the Supreme Court

Justice Brett Kavanaugh has worried about a scenario in which “thousands of absentee ballots flow in after election day and potentially flip the results of an election.” But this isn’t the case at all—there’s no result to flip until those ballots have been tallied
Nonetheless, his colleague Samuel Alito wrote in a June dissent in Watson v

Republican National Committee that “allowing absentee ballots to pour in over the days and weeks after election day, by which point preliminary election returns are being publicly reported,” might risk “undermining the public’s confidence in election integrity.” Maybe these misunderstandings would be rarer if Supreme Court justices weren’t encouraging them
Finally, and relatedly, keep in mind that we may not really know how the election turned out for days, or even weeks
In 2018, polling predicted a “blue wave” for Democrats, but on the night of the election, their victory seemed modest —certainly short of some of the most favorable predictions
Over the following 10 days, more and more races were called for Democrats, eventually producing the party’s biggest gain since Watergate
The outcomes of some races will not be clear tonight or tomorrow, and when they eventually are, they may not break entirely or even predominantly for either party
That uncertainty may feel uncomfortable, but it beats putting a lot of emotion into a result that isn’t real
Related: Brace for the blue shift ( From 2020 ) The Trump aide trying to stop a blue wave

title: Things Are Going to Get Ugly
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
If he loses control of one chamber of Congress, never mind both, the world will see a personality collapse and rage meltdown on the scale of the final sequence of the Lord of the Rings
The Donald Trump of 2018 could cope, barely
Back then, he had a number of things going for him
First, although Republicans suffered heavy losses in the House, they gained two seats in the Senate

Trump interpreted the Senate gains as proof that “people like me,” and the House losses as a rebuke to Trump-disloyal Republicans. “Mia Love,” he said of a Republican who lost her seat in Utah, “gave me no love, but then she lost
Too bad.” Second, the Trump of 2018 had the benefit of a strong economy
The war he was fighting in Iraq and Syria was going well and commanded broad bipartisan support, given that it had started under President Obama
Third, Trump did not have a lot personally at stake in the election of 2018
The big threat to him that year was the investigation of his Russia connections by Special Counsel Robert Mueller
The Mueller investigation was conducted within the executive branch
That investigation had been initiated even though the Republicans held the House, and Trump was later able to contain the damage from the investigation even though Republicans lost the House
Fourth, Trump in 2018 was younger, nimbler, and planning for the future: his reelection race in 2020
But if the most recent ones are accurate, the Trump of 2026 faces big losses in both chambers, all of them directly implicating him
The president opened a Senate seat in North Carolina by harrying the incumbent Republican, Thom Tillis, into retirement

Former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, now appears headed to a victory so big that he may flip the state legislature too, potentially upending one of the most successful Republican congressional gerrymanders
In the race for Ohio governor, Trump endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy, whose noxious campaign may cost the GOP not only another Senate seat, but the state legislature too
Trump even put a Senate seat in Texas in play by favoring the radioactive Ken Paxton over the popular incumbent, John Cornyn
Trump also started a war with Iran that he is not winning
He imposed tariffs that have raised prices and hurt farmers

He accelerated inflation with the deficits exacerbated by his so-called big, beautiful bill. [ Read: Trump is closing from behind ] The Trump of 2026 has a lot at stake in today’s unignorable election
The second Trump administration is a network of scandals and corruption
Subpoena power in the hands of his opponents will expose Trump and his family to enormous legal and political risk
Unlike in 2018, large numbers of Americans connect Trump’s self-enrichment to their economic decline
Gallup found that 89 percent of Americans agree that corruption is widespread in government, up 10 points from just a year ago, and up 30 points from 20 years ago
That’s far higher than in any other developed country, comparable to levels found in Lebanon, Peru, Ghana, and Nigeria
The Trump of 2026 is more addled and more clumsy than the Trump of 2018
In his final preelection speech, he reminded voters of his botched renovation of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.—and mused about renaming the pool after himself
Trump’s style of politics is authoritarian
He blatantly favored disaster-aid requests from states with Republican governors over those from states with Democratic governors
He was more likely to apportion tariff relief to firms that donated to Republicans, and more likely to refuse relief to firms that did not

When he encountered opposition in Congress, he responded with insults that permanently alienated legislators whose help he might need later. [ Peter Wehner: The MAGA reckoning arrives ] Trump ruled his party by fear, and now the fear is ebbing

On Sunday, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis made a campaign appearance near Mar-a-Lago to call on Republicans to take concerns about rising gas prices seriously—a cost most Americans blame on Trump’s Iran war
On November 1, the commentator Tucker Carlson posted on X a claim that Trump was planning a nuclear strike on Iran—and that only Vice President Vance and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stood in his way
Somebody who supports Vance is leaking to enhance his appeal at the expense of the president
Trump will not respond patiently to such challenges from within
He holds hundreds of millions of dollars in his MAGA super PAC and related entities
Whatever remains after the races this year could then go toward sustaining the Trump family’s political power—conceivably backing a future presidential bid by one of Trump’s children
If the Democrats take the House and subpoenas start arriving, Trump will still retain control of the U.S. military and U.S. security services
He can indict people, he can invade nations, he can invoke emergency powers

title: The Democrat Who’s Winning Over Voters in Trump Country
excerpt: C harles Benjamin voted for the first time in 2024, casting a ballot for President Trump
body: C harles Benjamin voted for the first time in 2024, casting a ballot for President Trump
Since then, he’s watched his McDonald’s order—two McDoubles and large fries—go up seven bucks

One of his fraternity brothers at East Stroudsburg University, who’s in the military, just shipped off to the Middle East to support a war that Benjamin believed Trump had promised not to start. “I don’t appreciate that he lied,” Benjamin, a 21-year-old junior sporting a leopard-print sweatshirt and holding a lacrosse stick, told me
I met Benjamin as he was waiting to see Josh Shapiro at a campus rally
Benjamin was curious about the Pennsylvania governor, but unsure whether to vote for him
A few dozen people stood around a small stage set out on the quad as students walked to class behind them, ignoring the speeches from local Democratic officials

He talked about high prices and the Iran war and corruption among elected officials. “I understand that there are some of you who showed up today with a little bit of healthy cynicism, a little bit of healthy skepticism, wondering, Is anything ever really going to change? ” Shapiro said
Yes, he told the crowd—but only if you care, and only if you vote
Benjamin and his friend Nick Vyprynyuk, a volunteer firefighter with disheveled strawberry-blond hair who had also cast his ballot for Trump in 2024, listened carefully

He was “electrifying,” Vyprynyuk, a senior, told me. “I like how enthusiastic he was.” Michelle Gustafson for The Atlantic Supporters cheer as Governor Josh Shapiro speaks at the Flip PA-01 Rally with Bob Harvie in Doylestown, Pennsylvania

Shapiro’s exuberance on the stump, in speeches that channel the optimistic pragmatism of former President Obama (not to mention his speaking cadence ), could help explain the Democratic governor’s popularity in Pennsylvania, a state that voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024
Shapiro has been able to feed deep-blue Democrats’ loathing of Trump while assembling a coalition that is large enough to include people who voted for the president

It’s an effective strategy: Polls regularly show him leading Republican Stacy Garrity, the MAGA-aligned state treasurer, by more than 20 points. (Garrity is pledging to “fix the problems Josh Shapiro has created,” including Pennsylvania’s relatively high tax burden and rising food prices.) Shapiro’s lead is larger than his margin of victory in 2022 against State Senator Doug Mastriano, who had a history of espousing far-right conspiracy theories and associating with Islamophobes and anti-Semites
Shapiro spent last week touring the state, with a focus on trying to win over rural voters—though actual Republicans tended to be elusive at his rallies
In Pike County, the ruby-red gateway to the Poconos, Trump won by 24 points two years ago
Few, if any, of the president’s supporters showed up to see the governor

In Milford, a tiny town in the state’s northeast corner, it was die-hard Democrats only—including the organizer of the town’s self-proclaimed “Resistance Committee,” a group that spends Wednesday afternoons in the center of town protesting Trump, and a guy in a Grateful Dead–themed Make America Grateful Again sweatshirt

Shapiro told people to take two signs on their way out—one to stick in their front yard that day, and another to replace it a day or two later, after their neighbors steal the first. “Smile when you put it back out there,” Shapiro said. “That sends a message to your neighbors: You’re not going to be messed with.” Even when Trump acolytes don’t show up, Shapiro is trying to send a message to rural voters: I’m looking out for you
Inside an old hunting and fishing lodge in Pennsylvania coal country, Shapiro bragged about ending the state’s century-old ban on hunting on Sundays

When he appeared at a small gym at a community college near Wilkes-Barre, Shapiro boasted of writing an executive order that heavily regulates the construction of AI data centers after hearing from concerned residents of a nearby community. [ From the November 2026 issue: The great data-center rebellion ] Shapiro’s campaign slogan is GSD, for “get shit done,” and that message plays to a broad swath of the state, said Danny Ceisler, the Democratic sheriff of Bucks County

He told me that Shapiro is “the antidote to what everybody hates about politics.” Ceisler unseated a Republican incumbent in the purple suburban county last year after criticizing his decision to partner with ICE
Ceisler said Shapiro’s ability to make things happen—including hiring more cops statewide—has earned him the respect and support of many law-enforcement officers
Michelle Gustafson for The Atlantic Shapiro greets attendees of the Montgomery County Grassroots Rally in Gilbertsville, Pennsylvania
Shapiro told me that achieving success as a Democrat in a purple state really is as straightforward as getting shit done. “Show up, especially in communities that didn’t vote for you
Listen to them and maybe why they made a different choice, and then do
Go back to the office and deliver for them,” he said outside the hunting lodge, which was in Schuylkill County and surrounded by crisp red-and-yellow maple leaves
It’s not a very satisfying answer—and it sounds a lot like what all politicians say is a winning formula
But Shapiro is betting that he can make that message resonate outside of his own race—and far beyond Pennsylvania
Four more years in Harrisburg to keep GSD-ing looks like a given, so he’s using his campaign to try to flip four swing congressional districts in Pennsylvania
Shapiro has tied his political future to the success of Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Janelle Stelson in south-central Pennsylvania, Bob Harvie in Bucks County, and Bob Brooks in the Lehigh Valley
They’re all Democrats trying to defeat incumbent Republican members of Congress
The effort is personal for Shapiro, who took credit for recruiting the Democrats to run
If he can help pull them over the line, he’ll have significant bragging rights for 2026—and one more achievement to tout if, as expected, he runs for president in 2028
S hapiro’s all-in support for the four is as telling as his calculations about which Democratic candidates not to fully back

At the hunting lodge in Schuylkill County, he spoke at the same event as Rachel Wallace, a Democrat running against Republican Dan Meuser. (Meuser accused Shapiro of lying about cuts to food assistance and health insurance in his speech at the lodge, claiming his remarks show a “lack of moral character.”) But Meuser’s seat is considered safe—he won by more than 40 points two years ago—and Shapiro knows it
He said he wants to see Wallace win but did not give her the kind of full-throttle endorsement he gave the other four
He recently created a federal political-action committee so he could funnel donations to the candidates he’s supporting, and Wallace is not among them
The vibe is different for the candidates he wants to help win; Shapiro often notes that Democrats need just four seats to flip control in the House

Standing beside Cognetti last week in Milford, he told the crowd, “You have the ability, by electing her, to literally put the Democrats in charge of the Congress and deliver a check against this president.” The next night, he told 200 people in a Teamsters parking lot that electing Stelson—a former Lancaster news anchor who narrowly lost a congressional race against the same competitor, the incumbent Scott Perry, two years ago—“quite literally will tilt the balance of power in Washington.” Michelle Gustafson for The Atlantic Campaign signs outside the Bucks County Democratic Committee office in Doylestown, Pennsylvania As I followed Shapiro’s bus tour through the Poconos and the Blue Mountains, I asked Cognetti, Stelson, and Wallace about how Shapiro—an anti-Trump Democrat from the liberal Philadelphia suburbs who spends a good portion of every speech slamming the president’s “chaos, cruelty, and corruption”—has won the backing of so many Republicans. (A New York Times /Siena poll in September found Shapiro winning support from a fifth of self-identified Republican voters.) Cognetti told me it’s because Shapiro is not a partisan in the way he governs; he appointed Republicans to his administration and has worked with the Republican-controlled state Senate

She’s been trying to convince voters that she does the same. “He doesn’t run the government of Pennsylvania in a hyper-partisan way,” she told me in a classroom at East Stroudsburg. “Similarly, I don’t run the city of Scranton in a partisan way.” Wallace, a longtime Democratic staffer who returned to Schuylkill County a few years ago when her mom was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, told me the lesson she takes from Shapiro is to show up

title: Latinos Are Still Swing Voters
excerpt: Latinos swung further toward Republicans than any other group in 2024, and they could swing further in the opposite direction this year
body: Latinos swung further toward Republicans than any other group in 2024, and they could swing further in the opposite direction this year
If Democrats recover the ground they have lost with this bloc over the past decade, it won’t mean that Latinos have come back to their natural political home
Like many Latinos, I’ve grown tired of having to talk every cycle about whether we lean Democrat or Republican

Are Latinos Democrats, because we support immigrants and workers’ rights? Are we Republicans, because our faith leads us to embrace traditional family values? I expected Donald Trump’s historic success among Latinos in 2024 to prompt fresh thinking about who Latinos are as a community—to foster a deeper understanding of what it means to be Latino, contradictions and all

In 2024, virtually every segment of the Latino population moved to the right—women and men, Catholics and evangelical Protestants, rich and poor, white and nonwhite, in cities and rural areas, the recently naturalized and longtime citizens

Trump energized new Latino voters who hadn’t participated in politics before, and although he may have been the main attraction, other Republicans also did better with Latinos than they had in previous elections
The elections of 2022 and 2024 brought many new Latino faces to Congress, and they came from all over the map
In addition to Latino representatives from Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, New Mexico, and Texas, we had others from New Jersey, Ohio, Oregon, and Washington
They were men and women, Democrats and Republicans
They were mechanics, organizers, business owners, veterans
They had varied interests and didn’t speak with one voice
They were a demonstration of how Latinos were as integrated into American politics as any other group

But two years later, many political observers still see Latinos as one-dimensional actors: as immigrants themselves, or as people instinctively inclined to sympathize with immigrants, or as traitors who are turning our backs to them
The focus on immigration makes sense, up to a point

The border is more secure today than it was under Joe Biden, but instead of dangerous criminals, the targets of ICE arrests have overwhelmingly been law-abiding, if undocumented, immigrants. [ Nick Miroff: Losing the ‘big-ass truck’ vote ] Yet even though Latinos as a group seem likely to vote against Republicans as a reaction against Trump’s immigration and economic policies, Democrats haven’t yet come to a consensus on exactly what immigration and economic policies we will be voting for

In terms of immigration, is it legalization? The end of private detention facilities? The continued deportation of dangerous criminals, but not law-abiding immigrants—à la Barack Obama, whom the left maligned as the deporter in chief? In terms of the economy, is it universal health care? A raised minimum wage? Programs to help Latinos start businesses? Taxing billionaires? The lesson that Democrats seem to have drawn from 2024 is that immigration isn’t a winning issue for them, so they’d better focus on inflation and the cost of living instead
Republicans, meanwhile, want to believe that Latinos care about the economy above all else, because that would give them cover to do whatever they want on immigration
That did seem to be the lesson of 2020 and 2024, when Trump did better and better among Latinos despite his draconian support for mass deportation

Most Latinos favor comprehensive immigration reform and think it’s wrong to deport immigrants who don’t have a criminal record and who have bought homes, raised families, and otherwise integrated into their communities

As the political scientist Matt Barreto told me before the 2024 election, Latinos want the border to be secure, but also think law-abiding immigrants who are longtime residents should be able to legalize

A comprehensive policy based on this distinction is tricky, though, because it leaves unresolved the question of what to do with recent unauthorized arrivals who are both hardworking and law-abiding, which is to say most of them

Since the mass deportations of Trump’s second administration began, we’ve upheld veterans and their families, or immigrants who arrived decades ago and have built a life here, as sympathetic characters unjustly caught up in Trump’s immigration dragnet

But does this mean we should be deporting hardworking immigrants who arrived more recently? Immigrants who came decades ago were new arrivals once, and new arrivals today will one day be immigrants who have been here for a long time
A poll in September, from NBC and Telemundo, showed significant divides within the Latino community on these and other questions
I was surprised to learn how minimally Latinos’ views of immigration have changed over the past few years—even after the arrests, deportations, and killings
When it came to “dealing with immigration,” respondents, by a margin of 45 to 31 percent, said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans

In 2022, that margin was 41 percent to 30 percent in favor of Democrats—that is, only a slightly higher percentage of Hispanics today think Democrats would handle immigration better. [ From the March 2022 Issue: There’s no such thing as ‘the Latino vote’ ] Thirty-eight percent of Latinos believe that Democrats would more effectively secure the border, while an equal percentage believe the reverse
Four years ago, Democrats had an 11-point advantage on that question

Moreover, a lower percentage of Latinos today think immigration “helps more than hurts,” and a higher percentage thinks immigration “hurts more than helps.” Finally, compared with four years ago, a lower percentage of Latinos think that immigrants brought to the United States when they were kids should be legalized, and about the same percentage—39 percent in 2024, 37 percent today—think that all undocumented immigrants should be deported

Democrats still have a lot of work to do to regain Latinos’ trust on immigration and the border, and Republicans haven’t suffered nearly as much as one might have expected given the Trump administration’s ruthlessness and cruelty
Latinos are clearly dissatisfied with Trump
The economy was one of his greatest strengths but is now a significant weakness for him
Like all Americans, Latinos say they want the price of food, gas, rent, health care, and other basic needs to be lower
They also want more and better jobs, and higher wages, and for mortgage interest rates to be lower, so they can afford to buy their own home
But they also like Trump’s no-tax-on-tips, overtime-pay, and Social Security policies, and they still generally see Republicans as the pro-business party

An important exception to the almost-exclusive focus on immigration and the economy is the work that Carlos Odio and Rachel Stein, of the Latino research and polling firm Equis , are doing in their newsletter, The New Dynamic

In addition to these issues, they have focused on the Iran war and the strong preference Latinos have for not getting entangled in foreign conflicts more generally, their objection to foreign aid if the trade-off is less investment at home, and the steadfast belief among Latinos, especially more recent arrivals, that the United States is the greatest country in the world

The goal should be not only to “ see with clear eyes what has been revealed in the age of Trump,” as they have written, but also to explore the broad array of issues that shaped Latino life and politics even before Trump entered the arena

For too long, this more expansive approach has been obscured or overshadowed by the issues of immigration and the economy, which can reveal as much about the partisan imperatives of the moment as about Latinos

After last spring’s primaries in Texas, Voto Latino, a Latino voter-mobilization group, asserted that Latinos are “ coming home to Democrats—there is no question about it .” When I mentioned this to Daniel Garza, a longtime Republican and head of the conservative LIBRE Initiative, he said, “There is no home for Latinos.” My hope is that Latinos will claim many political homes instead of just one, and that candidates in all parties continue to fight for votes that we will give them only if they represent the interests of the many communities we are a part of, then follow through on their promises.

title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
excerpt: Rules over reasoning: Instead of trying to peer inside AI "brains" to ensure good behavior, a growing group of researchers wants to design incentive systems tha
body: Rules over reasoning: Instead of trying to peer inside AI "brains" to ensure good behavior, a growing group of researchers wants to design incentive systems that make following the rules the most rational choice—regardless of what's actually happening under the hood

Catching AI playing dumb: One proposed trick involves rewarding models not just for test performance, but for how well their answers predict what a second model would say—making deliberate underperformance a losing strategy

Cops, citizens, and collusion: Princeton's Elad Hazan envisions AI models taking turns as "solvers" and "auditors," borrowing from human systems like law enforcement—though the risk of agents colluding remains a real and unsolved problem

The market may be the biggest obstacle: Even a perfectly aligned AI could lose out if it's slower or costlier than a less scrupulous competitor—raising the uncomfortable question of whether the real mechanism in need of a redesign is the free market itself. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147934" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear
Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code

The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .  Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results

Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces
This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible

Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest
Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned

This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.  A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).  Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say

Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.  The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.  A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.  During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters

In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.  There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals

But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.  Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s
Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said
Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer

Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.  Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know

Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally

Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.  It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable

AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.  “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior
Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them
But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models
It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice

Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)  Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan

A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?  “It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that

But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada
AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week
It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself

The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities
The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites
Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period
A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology

A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents)
As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue
One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up
Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary
It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too
In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms

But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated

The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia

But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently
But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway
Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI

Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too
One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars
It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change
But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand

And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month
But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money
Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI

The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change
If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case

It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.  Midterm elections are tomorrow
Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy)
We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives
Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/12/ftc-issues-opinion-order-against-cambridge-analytica-deceiving-consumers-about-collection-facebook">deceptively</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-cambridge-analyticas-facebook-targeting-model-really-worked-according-to-the-person-who-built-it-94078">used data from Facebook users</a> without their permission to create <a href="https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/psychographics">psychographic</a> profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.</p>

<p>But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/jan/04/cambridge-analytica-data-leak-global-election-manipulation">exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears</a> and <a href="https://www.channel4.com/news/revealed-trump-campaign-strategy-to-deter-millions-of-black-americans-from-voting-in-2016">discouraging them from voting</a>.</p>

<p>I’m <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=5YUMd8EAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">a political communication scholar</a> who <a href="https://emma-briant.co.uk/">studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare</a>. My research <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2018/apr/20/cambridge-analytica-propaganda-machine">helped expose</a> the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2018/apr/16/fake-news-inquiry-raises-concerns-over-targeting-of-voters-in-brexit-referendum">The Guardian’s reporting</a> on whistelblower accounts and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2018/nov/17/arron-banks-emails-steve-bannon-brexit-campaign-funds">the evidence</a> I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to <a href="https://committees.parliament.uk/committee/378/digital-culture-media-and-sport-committee/news/103479/fake-news-briant-evidence-17-19/">parliamentary</a> and <a href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/cambridge-analytica-and-the-future-of-data-privacy">congressional investigations</a>. I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely. </p>

<p>My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data. </p>

<h2>Investigative failures</h2>

<p>The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse. </p>

<p>The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in <a href="https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-documents-report-volume5.pdf">its final report</a> that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”</p>

<p>The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data. </p>

<p>At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-15294-7_7">use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior</a> focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S.</p>

            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Q91nvbJSmS4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Facebook user data was at the heart of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “<a href="https://www.sphere-abacus.com/programme/13/people-you-may-know">People You May Know</a>,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. </p>

<p>The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about <a href="https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/10/meta-whines-new-mexico-is-impossible-to-please-after-historic-25-billion-fine/">thousands of applications associated with data misuse</a>. Meta said it would appeal the decision.</p>

<p>Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.</p>

<h2>Escaping further scrutiny</h2>

<p>Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated. </p>

<p>In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, <a href="https://www.techpolicy.press/the-459-million-cambridge-analytica-reckoning-buried-in-metas-teen-safety-settlement/">Meta settled</a> with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an <a href="https://www.techpolicy.press/the-459-million-cambridge-analytica-reckoning-buried-in-metas-teen-safety-settlement/">allocation of $459.3 million</a> to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states. </p>

<p>The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” <a href="https://www.mass.gov/doc/meta-settlement/download?">release Meta</a> from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.</p>

<p>A decade-old matter - Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal - was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.</p>

<p>From the <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/07/ftc-imposes-5-billion-penalty-sweeping-new-privacy-restrictions-facebook">2019 Federal Trade Commission order</a> to the <a href="https://www.classaction.org/media/in-re-facebook-inc-consumer-privacy-user-profile-litigation-settlement-agreement.pdf">2022 class action settlement</a> to <a href="https://theconversation.com/changes-to-facebook-and-instagram-are-key-part-of-metas-17b-settlement-with-the-states-over-harm-to-teens-290582">August 2026’s multistate deal</a>, settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.</p>

<p>Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the <a href="https://www.internationalaffairs.org.au/australianoutlook/in-fighting-the-disinformation-problem-we-risk-losing-the-battle-for-our-minds-to-big-tech/">lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation</a>, but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “<a href="https://lnkd.in/p/gG26b3Xp">We’re just getting started</a>.” </p>

<p>Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “<a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/public_statements/1536911/chopra_dissenting_statement_on_facebook_7-24-19.pdf">Facebook’s unjust enrichment</a>.” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.</p>

<h2>What price for the harm?</h2>

<p>The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.</p>

<p>If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win. </p>

<p>The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295620/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
