<title>Pediatric palliative care addresses the unique needs of seriously ill children and their families</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769648/original/file-20261102-64-mke5f0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Children with life-threatening conditions need a different kind of care than other patients do.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/top-view-of-a-nurse-comforting-a-little-girl-royalty-free-image/2172538976">Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pediatric medicine generally entails caring for patients at the beginning of their lives – performing newborn checkups, treating childhood illnesses and supporting adolescents in their health as they move toward adulthood.  </p>

<p>So people are often surprised to hear about <a href="https://med.emory.edu/directory/profile/?u=KJOHN31">specialists like us</a> <a href="https://med.emory.edu/departments/pediatrics/divisions/palliative-care/profile/?u=ECFLYNN">who work in</a> <a href="https://www.who.int/europe/news-room/fact-sheets/item/palliative-care-for-children">pediatric palliative care</a>, helping children facing serious illness who may be nearing the end of their lives.</p>

<p>This approach to care focuses on relieving suffering and addressing quality of life for children and families facing complex, life-limiting medical conditions. We also work to ensure that every family who needs it has access to this care, because right now, these programs aren’t available to most families globally who need them.</p>

<h2>Holistic, empathetic care</h2>

<p>Pediatric palliative care is an approach that emerged out of the <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6179468/">adult hospice and palliative care movement</a> in the 1990s to early 2000s as a distinct discipline.</p>

<p>Globally, an estimated <a href="https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/topic-details/GHO/child-mortality-and-causes-of-death">7 million children die annually</a>. Children with life-threatening health conditions often <a href="https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10390/chapter/1">live longer between the time of diagnosis and death</a> than adults. They benefit from approaches to care that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2023.1602">consider the needs of their caregivers and family members</a>.</p>

<p>Pediatric palliative care is provided by a team of professionals, including physicians, nurses, social workers, child life specialists, chaplains and other allied health professionals who take a comprehensive approach to a child’s care as they live with serious illness and ultimately approach the end of their life. The goal of this care is to support families in making every day as good as it possibly can be, regardless of whether or not a child’s life remaining is short. At the heart of this approach is the belief that <a href="https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/convention-text">each child has a right</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2007.02.022">holistic, empathetic care during illness and throughout end of their life</a> that considers their unique social, cultural, physical and spiritual needs.</p>

<p>For example, an infant who is diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder that affects vital organ function and shortens life expectancy may need to be in and out of the hospital to manage acute illnesses and complex symptoms, such as pain and difficulty breathing. In turn, her parents may need help with deciding which treatments will be most helpful or may cause more suffering than benefit.</p>

<p>A palliative care team works with patients and caregivers to formulate a plan that ensures this baby gets care that affords her opportunities to experience as many happy moments as possible. This can improve the lived experience of this child and her parents.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/EL11DMMYxIU?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A good palliative care clinician can help parents understand the importance of protecting their terminally ill child from painful and ineffective medical interventions.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Avoiding unnecessary care</h2>

<p>Children and families who have benefited from pediatric palliative care describe these services as <a href="https://www.ninr.nih.gov/sites/default/files/NINR_508c_FamilyStories_0.pdf">the supportive lifeline</a> that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/27/well/live/for-kids-with-cancer-focusing-on-quality-of-life.html">helped them to navigate</a> the complexities of diagnosis, <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2014/01/20/lives-less-ordinary">life with serious illness</a> and, ultimately, death and bereavement.</p>

<p>Over the past 20 years, there has been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1089/jpm.2018.0483">growing evidence</a> suggesting the benefits of this approach. Children who receive care from pediatric palliative care specialists have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2019.08.005">less pain, nausea and other distressing symptoms</a> that can affect their day-to-day function and overall quality of life.</p>

<p>Research also shows that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/PCC.0000000000000209">children admitted to intensive care settings</a> for managing life-threatening illness are more likely to receive care that aligns with their goals. When a palliative care specialist is consulted, patients are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1089/jpm.2018.0292">less likely to opt for life-sustaining therapies</a> that would not change their long-term prognosis.</p>

<h2>The US on the cutting edge</h2>

<p>The U.S. is on the global forefront of pediatric palliative care: Nearly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2020-021634">80% of U.S. children’s hospitals</a> have formal, interdisciplinary programs to provide this specialized care. But access to services in a clinic setting or at home is less consistent. Not every hospital-based palliative care program is connected to outpatient or home-based services, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2025.08.004">creating gaps for patients and families</a> who need to access this supportive care between hospitalizations. </p>

<p>Generally, palliative care in the U.S. is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2025.08.004">more readily available in urban settings</a> and at academic medical centers than in rural areas and community hospitals. These differences are <a href="https://scorecard.capc.org/">most pronounced in rural states and the Southeast</a>, a region of the country that has historically had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01495-8">health disparities across racial and socioeconomic differences</a>. It can be difficult for children in these places to access patient-centered, interdisciplinary supportive services. </p>

<h2>Global disparities</h2>

<p>Outside the U.S., pediatric palliative care can be even more difficult to access. Though it’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2016.08.020">hard to measure</a>, estimates suggest that more than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-024-01539-8">21 million children worldwide would benefit</a> from a pediatric palliative care approach.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2025.07.026">More than half of the world’s population</a> live in countries where the availability of any palliative care is defined as either emerging or progressing, according to the World Health Organization. Only 14% of countries – 28 total – are considered to have advanced levels of palliative care development. The numbers are fairly similar for pediatrics, with one study identifying <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/children12040440">only 11 countries as reaching the highest level</a> of pediatric palliative care development.</p>

<p><iframe id="N9ANc" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/N9ANc/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Map of the world showing countries in four different colors based on their level of palliative care development: emerging, progressive, established and advanced."></iframe></p>

<p>As many as <a href="https://thewhpca.org/resources/global-atlas-of-palliative-care-2nd-ed-2020/">97% of children</a> in need of this approach <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2015-308307">live in low- and middle-income countries</a>. Children in these countries have less access to medical diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and are often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00757-8">diagnosed at later stages of illness</a> with less access to curative therapy.</p>

<p>The types of pediatric serious illnesses seen in the developing world are also very different from the landscape in the U.S. The greatest need for pediatric palliative care in developing nations – about 30% of cases – is in <a href="https://thewhpca.org/resources/global-atlas-of-palliative-care-2nd-ed-2020/">children with HIV</a>. Among other <a href="https://thewhpca.org/resources/global-atlas-of-palliative-care-2nd-ed-2020/">children needing palliative care</a>, about 18% are living with complications from prematurity, roughly 16% suffer from congenital malformations, and about 16% are dealing with injuries leading to severe neurologic impairment.</p>

<p>In contrast to many high-income settings, <a href="https://thewhpca.org/resources/global-atlas-of-palliative-care-2nd-ed-2020/">children with malignant diseases</a> such as leukemias and solid tumors represent a relatively small proportion – about 4% – of patients who would benefit from a palliative care approach. In these regions, the predominant ailments are HIV/AIDS, premature birth and birth trauma, congenital anomalies and injuries.</p>

<h2>Filling in the care gaps</h2>

<p>In low- and middle-income countries, essential medications like morphine, used for controlling pain and other symptoms, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2024.10.026">often aren’t available</a>. In addition, healthcare workers often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/02692163251348091">haven’t been trained</a> in <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/palliative-care">foundational principles of palliative care</a>.</p>

<p>On top of that, many of these countries don’t have the political infrastructure to <a href="https://sdgs.un.org/goals">provide basic healthcare</a>, much less facilitate developing a comprehensive palliative care program for children.</p>

<p>The good news is that there are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-025-01837-9">existing models</a> for countries that are starting from scratch to build upon. And there’s room for innovation. Established <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-024-10920-5">community partnerships and technologies</a> can be leveraged in new ways – for instance, using online learning and video conferencing to help train healthcare workers and build relationships.</p>

<p>We believe pediatric palliative care is the heart of what healthcare should be when a child faces a serious, life-limiting illness, regardless of where they live in the world. Because even when medicine cannot cure, it can always heal and comfort.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286905/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

When a palliative care specialist is consulted, patients are less likely to opt for life-sustaining therapies that would not change their long-term prognosis

The US on the cutting edge The U.S. is on the global forefront of pediatric palliative care: Nearly 80% of U.S. children’s hospitals have formal, interdisciplinary programs to provide this specialized care
But access to services in a clinic setting or at home is less consistent

Not every hospital-based palliative care program is connected to outpatient or home-based services, creating gaps for patients and families who need to access this supportive care between hospitalizations
Generally, palliative care in the U.S. is more readily available in urban settings and at academic medical centers than in rural areas and community hospitals
These differences are most pronounced in rural states and the Southeast , a region of the country that has historically had health disparities across racial and socioeconomic differences
It can be difficult for children in these places to access patient-centered, interdisciplinary supportive services

Though it’s hard to measure , estimates suggest that more than 21 million children worldwide would benefit from a pediatric palliative care approach
More than half of the world’s population live in countries where the availability of any palliative care is defined as either emerging or progressing, according to the World Health Organization
Only 14% of countries – 28 total – are considered to have advanced levels of palliative care development
The numbers are fairly similar for pediatrics, with one study identifying only 11 countries as reaching the highest level of pediatric palliative care development
As many as 97% of children in need of this approach live in low- and middle-income countries
Children in these countries have less access to medical diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and are often diagnosed at later stages of illness with less access to curative therapy
The types of pediatric serious illnesses seen in the developing world are also very different from the landscape in the U.S
The greatest need for pediatric palliative care in developing nations – about 30% of cases – is in children with HIV

Among other children needing palliative care , about 18% are living with complications from prematurity, roughly 16% suffer from congenital malformations, and about 16% are dealing with injuries leading to severe neurologic impairment

In contrast to many high-income settings, children with malignant diseases such as leukemias and solid tumors represent a relatively small proportion – about 4% – of patients who would benefit from a palliative care approach
In these regions, the predominant ailments are HIV/AIDS, premature birth and birth trauma, congenital anomalies and injuries

<title>Menopause can quietly weaken bones – here’s what research reveals about protecting them</title>
    <content type="html"><p>A skeleton hanging on a door or standing in your neighbor’s yard for Halloween looks like a finished structure. But the skeleton inside a living body is constantly changing. Around menopause, those changes can tip toward bone loss, often without pain or another obvious warning.</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://orthopaedicresearch.wustl.edu/labs/naomi-dirckx/meet-the-dirckx-lab/">skeletal biology researcher</a> at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. My work examines how hormonal and metabolic signals influence bone renewal. In my assessment, the quiet nature of bone loss makes menopause an important time to bring skeletal health into the conversation.</p>

<p>Bone loss can start accelerating before the final menstrual period. Natural menopause is confirmed only after <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/menopause/">12 consecutive months without a period</a>, when there is no other explanation. Bone loss can therefore accelerate before someone knows that their last period was their final one.</p>

<h2>Why bone changes during menopause</h2>

<p>Bones are <a href="https://theconversation.com/bones-communicate-with-the-rest-of-the-body-to-support-overall-health-heres-the-science-behind-your-skeleton-279735">living tissues that continually renew themselves</a>. During this process, called remodeling, cells known as <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/24871-osteoblasts-and-osteoclasts">osteoclasts</a> remove old bone while other cells – osteoblasts – build its replacement. Estrogen helps regulate this renewal. As estrogen levels decline around menopause, removal can outpace replacement, contributing to <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis">bone loss and osteoporosis</a>, a condition in which bones become more fragile and porous.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis">Osteoporosis</a> can affect women and men. It becomes more common with age but can also occur in younger people. A person often has no noticeable symptoms until a fracture occurs.</p>

<p>The timing is revealing. An analysis of 862 participants in the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.534">Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation</a>, a long-term U.S. study of women in midlife, tracked changes in bone density in relation to their final menstrual period. On average, loss at the lower spine and near the hip was fastest from about one year before that period through two years afterward. It then slowed rather than stopped.</p>

<p>These findings do not mean that everyone experiences the same amount of bone loss or develops osteoporosis. They show why the menopausal transition itself deserves attention, rather than treating bone loss as a concern only for older women.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Cartoon-style infographic of three women and small close-ups of different levels of bone health, from normal to severe osteoporosis." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=895&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=895&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=895&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1124&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1124&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769152/original/file-20261029-64-9k3uir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1124&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Fracture risk and bone loss involve more than age</h2>

<p>To assess a person’s risk of breaking a bone, clinicians consider factors such as low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol use and whether a patient’s parent experienced a hip fracture. A <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis/diagnosis-treatment-and-steps-to-take">bone density scan</a> measures bone mineral density and helps assess fracture risk. It provides useful information alongside medical history and other risk factors.</p>

<p>The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an independent panel of experts in preventive care, <a href="https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening">recommends screening for osteoporosis</a> in women age 65 and older. It also recommends screening younger postmenopausal women when their health history and other risk factors indicate a higher chance of a fracture. This does not mean every woman needs a scan as soon as her periods change.</p>

<p>These recommendations address routine screening. People who already have osteoporosis, have broken a bone after a minor fall or have a disease or take medicines that cause bone loss need evaluation tailored to their circumstances.</p>

<p>A U.K. trial illustrates how <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32640-5">identifying people at high risk and recommending treatment can help</a>. More than 12,000 women age 70 to 85 received either usual care or screening, followed by treatment recommendations for those at high risk. Over five years, women in the screening group were less likely to break a hip. However, when the researchers considered osteoporosis-related fractures across different parts of the body together, they did not find a statistically significant reduction. The findings support screening linked to treatment in older women, but do not tell us when screening should begin during the menopausal transition.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/yjCgUS_k-4w?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Bones are active organs that communicate with the rest of the body.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Movement and nutrition support the skeleton</h2>

<p>Bones respond to the forces placed on them. Weight-bearing activities such as walking and stair climbing make bones support the body’s weight. <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/exercise-your-bone-health">Resistance exercises</a> using weights, bands or body weight create additional forces on bones as muscles pull against them. Balance training, such as tai chi and exercises that practice shifting weight from one foot to the other, can improve stability and help prevent falls. Activity for bone health therefore involves more than one kind of movement.</p>

<p>An Australian trial published in 2018 tested whether supervised heavy resistance exercises and impact movements <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jbmr.3284">could improve bone density and physical function in postmenopausal women</a> with low bone mass. After eight months, participants in that program had better results than those following a less intensive home exercise program. The women were carefully screened, and the training was closely supervised.</p>

<p>These improvements are encouraging, but improved bone density is not the same outcome as fewer broken bones: The trial did not establish whether its program reduced fractures. People with osteoporosis, previous fractures or physical limitations may need guidance on appropriate movements and loads. Building muscle strength and balance can support mobility as well as bone health. <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/exercise-your-bone-health">Choosing suitable exercise</a> depends on a person’s own circumstances.</p>

<p>Nutrition contributes in a different way. Calcium supplies mineral that <a href="https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Calcium-Consumer/">helps give bones their strength</a>, while <a href="https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-HealthProfessional/">vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium</a>. Adequate protein also forms part of a balanced diet. Calcium-rich foods include dairy products, fortified alternatives, canned sardines or salmon with edible bones, and vegetables such as bok choy and broccoli.</p>

<p>Calcium or vitamin D supplements may help when a person’s intake is insufficient or they have a deficiency that needs treatment. They do not replace osteoporosis medicines when those are needed. <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis/diagnosis-treatment-and-steps-to-take">Nutrition and treatment</a> work together.</p>

<h2>Treatment depends on the person</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/gme.0000000000002028">Systemic menopausal hormone therapy</a> — treatment that delivers hormones throughout the body — can relieve bothersome hot flashes and night sweats and help prevent bone loss and fractures. Its benefits and risks depend on age, time since menopause, medical history and the treatment used.</p>

<p>For women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset who have no medical reasons to avoid it, the balance of benefits and risks from menopausal hormone therapy is generally favorable for treating troublesome symptoms and preventing bone loss. This does not mean hormone therapy is suitable for everyone. Patients and clinicians should discuss their symptoms, bone health and individual risks, and revisit the decision over time.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis/diagnosis-treatment-and-steps-to-take">Other osteoporosis medicines</a> can slow bone breakdown or stimulate bone formation. Clinicians also consider <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/osteoporosis">other medical conditions and medicines that can weaken bones</a>, including hormonal disorders, digestive conditions and long-term glucocorticoid treatment. Menopause may be only part of the explanation.</p>

<p>One example is <a href="https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/endocrine-diseases/primary-hyperparathyroidism">primary hyperparathyroidism</a>, in which one or more parathyroid glands in the neck produce too much parathyroid hormone. This can raise blood calcium and weaken bones. Identifying it can change the care plan. It illustrates why investigating the cause of bone loss matters, rather than simply attributing it to aging.</p>

<h2>Access to care matters, too</h2>

<p>Advice about scans and treatment assumes people can obtain them. Looking beyond individual choices shows how access to care can shape the options available. One example comes from a <a href="https://www.osteoporosis.foundation/asia-pacific-audit-2025">2025 audit of 22 Asia-Pacific countries and regions</a>. It documented substantial differences in access to osteoporosis care. Bone density scan waits ranged from the same day to nearly a year, and gaps in coverage for medicines limited the affordability of treatment. <a href="https://www.osteoporosis.foundation/news/tackling-burden-osteoporosis-and-fragility-fractures-apco-iof-asia-pacific-regional-audit">The regional audit</a> concerns osteoporosis broadly, not only menopause.</p>

<p>In other words, making prevention possible requires both public awareness and health systems that make scans, follow-up care and treatment accessible and affordable.</p>

<p>Menopause offers an opportunity to ask about the skeleton while a person still feels well. The answer may involve a risk assessment, suitable activity, nutritional changes or medical treatment. A bone health conversation can begin long before a fracture starts it.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293648/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: As it gets harder to figure out what to eat, some Americans are turning to religion for answers

<title>As it gets harder to figure out what to eat, some Americans are turning to religion for answers</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769106/original/file-20261029-64-exok6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Conflicting food advice is leaving shoppers confused.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/rear-view-of-young-woman-carrying-shopping-basket-royalty-free-image/2161809431?phrase=food%20choices%20healthy&amp;adppopup=true">Oscar Wong/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It’s getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week? </p>

<p>These questions make trips to the grocery store and mealtime decisions more difficult. For centuries, some people have turned to their religious texts and traditions for answers. </p>

<p>In “<a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/born-again-bodies/paper">Born Again Bodies</a>,” religious studies scholar <a href="https://rap.wustl.edu/people/r-marie-griffith/">R. Marie Griffith</a> traces how Protestant Christian ideas on faith and the body shaped the development of American diet and fitness culture.</p>

<p>Through my <a href="https://allegheny.edu/about/campus-department-resources/faculty-and-staff-directory/adrienne-krone/">decade of ethnographic research</a> on religious food movements, I have found that many Americans are still turning to religion as they decide what to eat. I analyzed four religious alternative food movements in my 2025 book, “<a href="https://uncpress.org/9781469690322/free-range-religion/">Free-Range Religion</a>.” I argue there that these movements aren’t just changing what they eat; they are working to reshape the American food system from the ground up.</p>

<h2>Jewish community farming</h2>

<p>Two of the sites I studied were Jewish farms that were providing experiential education opportunities for the local Jewish community. It was part of their larger mission to reconnect Jews to the land and to the agrarian roots of Judaism. They often point out that the ancient Israelites were an agrarian people and that many Jewish laws, values and holidays were shaped by that context. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A mound of dirt with a hen nearby." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769146/original/file-20261029-64-l9ky7x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A compost pile at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Adrienne Krone</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>At the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center in Falls Village, Connecticut, I worked alongside young Jewish adults participating in a three-month program, the <a href="https://adamah.org/isabella-freedman/farm-fellowship/?">Adamah Farm Fellowship</a>, as they planted, harvested and prepared produce for their weekly community supported agriculture program. The fellows begin their days with a morning prayer session and take time away from their work on the farm to celebrate Shabbat together. The fellows also attend classes where they learn about the biblical laws and ethical concepts related to agriculture, alongside scientific research on sustainable agriculture. </p>

<p>I conducted my fieldwork during a “shmita” year, <a href="https://journal.fi/scripta/article/view/67459">a year of rest for the land</a>. Just as the Hebrew Bible instructed Jews to work for six days and rest on Shabbat, the seventh day, they were also instructed to work their land for six years and then let it rest in the seventh year, the shmita year. </p>

<p>Farms took different approaches to the “shmita” year: The Adamah Farm Fellows kept their fields in production and started a community garden to mark their observance of the “shmita” year. At the <a href="https://www.pearlstonecenter.org/">Pearlstone center</a> in Reisterstown, Maryland, the farmers replaced their usual rows of vegetables with cover crops that would enrich the soil during its year of rest. They also canceled their community supported agriculture program and focused their educational programs on the Jewish texts and traditions of “shmita” and the importance of rest for all beings. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The farm at the Pearlstone retreat in Reisterstown, Md., during the ‘shmita’ year.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Adrienne Krone</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The Hallelujah Diet</h2>

<p>Another group I studied were followers of the Hallelujah Diet, a plant-based diet rooted in the biblical story of the Garden of Eden. In “<a href="https://openlibrary.org/books/OL8065637M/The_Hallelujah_Diet">The Hallelujah Diet</a>,” first published in 2006, the Rev. George Malkmus determined that the ideal food system was laid out in the first chapter of the Book of Genesis, <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%201%3A29&amp;version=KJV">where God instructs humans to eat plants, fruits and seeds</a>. In the Garden of Eden, Adam and Eve would not have had access to cooked food, so the Hallelujah Diet also prioritizes the consumption of raw, uncooked vegan foods. </p>

<p>I attended a Hallelujah Diet health retreat in Lake Lure, North Carolina, in 2015 with nine followers of the Hallelujah Diet. This was a small subset of Hallelujah dieters. In the summer of 2013, I attended a talk by George Malkmus in Charlotte, North Carolina, along with hundreds of Hallelujah dieters. </p>

<p>Religion scholar <a href="https://www.wm.edu/as/religiousstudies/faculty/blazer_a.php">Annie Blazer</a> found that followers of the Hallelujah Diet <a href="https://cup.columbia.edu/book/religion-food-and-eating-in-north-america/9780231160308/">tend to believe</a> that it will cure their ailments and help them lead long and healthy lives. I found that the reality is a bit more complicated.  </p>

<p>The retreat guests were adopting the diet in the hope that it would help them address medical issues, but they were not solely relying on the diet to heal them. The retreat guests were also seeing healthcare professionals and taking medications, recovering from or scheduling surgeries, and visiting physical therapists. </p>

<h2>Baldwin Beef</h2>

<p>The fourth site I studied was <a href="https://www.baldwinbeef.com/">Baldwin Beef</a>, a family-owned cattle farm that produced 100% grass-fed beef in Yanceyville, North Carolina. The Baldwins are Christian and raise their cows in line with their understanding that, according to the Bible, cows are meant to live on pasture and eat grass.  </p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large number of cows on a farm, with trees in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769143/original/file-20261029-64-bp6puy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cows at Baldwin Beef, a cattle farm in Yanceyville, N.C., which produces 100% grass-fed beef.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Adrienne Krone</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This differs from the more common practice in the United States of moving cattle to feedlots for their final months and <a href="https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09082026/blackshirt-building-nations-largest-beef-feedlot-in-nebraska/">feeding them grain</a>. The Baldwins also collaborated with a smaller-scale halal slaughterhouse to ensure that their cows experienced less stress in their final moments. </p>

<p>Christians and many other religious Americans have been wrestling with their <a href="https://www.routledge.com/Animals-and-Religion/Aftandilian-Ambros-Gross/p/book/9781032330181">relationship with animals and the ethics of eating meat</a> since the 19th century. Many contemporary religious and nonreligious movements are reconsidering current animal welfare practices. In some cases, this means advocacy for vegetarianism or veganism and in others it means working to address issues in animal agriculture. </p>

<h2>Free-range religion</h2>

<p>I use the term “free-range religion” in my book’s title for a reason: Americans belong to many communities at once, including religious communities, and the boundaries between communities are often porous. </p>

<p>For example, on the surface, the Hallelujah Diet book appears to be a Christian diet, written by a reverend. But I found that the reality was more complicated. </p>

<p>At the Hallelujah Diet health retreat I attended, all the participants were Christian – except for me, I’m Jewish – but the leaders of the retreat were <a href="https://www.bartehrman.com/messianic-judaism/">Messianic Jews</a>, who identify as Jews but believe Jesus was the Messiah. During our time at the retreat, we encountered a number of theological differences within our group, but our hosts encouraged us to remain focused on our shared interest in improving our bodily health. </p>

<p>In our educational sessions, medical doctors were cited as sources alongside biblical prophets, reflecting the range of authorities Hallelujah dieters recognize. The retreat participants similarly incorporated an array of practices into their daily lives, including yoga, meditation and the use of essential oils. </p>

<p>They saw some of these practices as part of their spiritual practice, while others were curtained off as “new age” and were seen as practices they engaged in outside of their Christianity. </p>

<h2>Food and purity</h2>

<p>As British anthropologist <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/biography/mary-douglas/">Mary Douglas</a> demonstrated many decades ago in “<a href="https://www.routledge.com/Purity-and-Danger-An-Analysis-of-Concepts-of-Pollution-and-Taboo/Douglas/p/book/9780415289955">Purity and Danger</a>,” religion plays a central role in food choices as communities make determinations about what is considered clean and unclean. For many religious communities, food rules bring them together through shared values and identities but also separate them from others. </p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Rainbow chard in a wash basin." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769144/original/file-20261029-64-pl0lhl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Produce at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Adrienne Krone</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>That is certainly happening today. Many communities still use food as a way to establish boundaries for membership. Jewish communities, for example, regularly establish rules around what people can bring to events to preserve the kosher status of synagogue kitchens. The kosher laws include restrictions on the types of meat that can be consumed and prohibits mixing meat and dairy in the same meal, so keeping a kitchen kosher requires communal adherence to these rules.  </p>

<p>But these food decisions are also bringing religious and nonreligious people together in interesting ways and creating new collaborations in their efforts to transform the food system. The Jewish farmers from Adamah and Pearlstone are now part of a large umbrella organization, <a href="https://adamah.org/">also called Adamah</a>, that engages in interfaith climate advocacy work at national and international levels.</p>

<p>All of the groups I studied identified a concern regarding the food system. For the Jewish farmers, it was that Jews had become disconnected from food production. For the Hallelujah dieters, it was a concern that people were not eating the diet that they believed humans were created by God to eat in the Garden of Eden. For the Baldwin family, it was a concern that modern beef production did not align with biblical descriptions of cattle grazing on green pastures. </p>

<p>For these religious people, the solution was to start a farm or a diet that would provide a pathway for people to choose a different relationship with food or food production. These groups started small, with changes to their individual diets and commitments that shape their own approaches to producing food, but they all aspire to improving the entire food system.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291119/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

A scroll through social media raises many questions

Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week? These questions make trips to the grocery store and mealtime decisions more difficult
For centuries, some people have turned to their religious texts and traditions for answers
In “ Born Again Bodies ,” religious studies scholar R
Marie Griffith traces how Protestant Christian ideas on faith and the body shaped the development of American diet and fitness culture
Through my decade of ethnographic research on religious food movements, I have found that many Americans are still turning to religion as they decide what to eat

I analyzed four religious alternative food movements in my 2025 book, “ Free-Range Religion .” I argue there that these movements aren’t just changing what they eat; they are working to reshape the American food system from the ground up

It was part of their larger mission to reconnect Jews to the land and to the agrarian roots of Judaism

<title>Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/641609/original/file-20250109-15-inhf9h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C24%2C8155%2C5432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some students can be aggressive if they don&#39;t like their grade.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/happy-university-students-raising-hands-on-a-class-royalty-free-image/2177185923">skynesher/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.67403/001c.172577">by their students over grades</a>, according to an international study <a href="https://www.adler.edu/faculty-engagement/faculty-directory/jason-walker/">I</a> conducted with colleagues <a href="https://www.ucanwest.ca/directory/dr-zahra-moradi">Zahra Moradi</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=XfvKveEAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">Deborah Circo</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Gradebook with written grades written in" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769330/original/file-20261030-64-1t3rml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Grades can lead to conflict.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/113026679@N03/23198966652">David Mulder/flickr</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Researchers <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph21091173">define workplace bullying</a> as <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/ca/workplace-bullying-and-mobbing-in-the-united-states-2-volumes-9781440850233/">harmful acts of mistreatment</a> between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.</p>

<p>Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are <a href="http://doi.org/10.1177/09500170221134397">Black, Indigenous or people of color</a> were targeted more frequently. </p>

<p>Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it <a href="http://doi.org/10.1080/19407882.2016.1199385">contrapower harassment</a> – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.</p>

<p>More than 30% of adult workers in <a href="https://workplacebullying.org/2024-wbi-us-survey/">the U.S.</a> and <a href="https://canadasafetycouncil.org/working-bully/">Canada</a> experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, <a href="http://doi.org/10.1080/02678373.2012.734709">harming both individuals and organizations</a>. </p>

<p>That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields <a href="http://doi.org/10.28933/ijprr-2020-01-1205">like emergency services</a>, according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Academic bullying <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-14625-2_50">undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity</a> of higher education institutions. </p>

<p>Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.</p>

<p>Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.</p>

<h2>How we did our work</h2>

<p>We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K. </p>

<p>Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Harassment doesn't always involve shouting. It can be quiet" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769329/original/file-20261030-78-8mp6ko.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A person sits in a chair facing an empty lecture hall.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/sixthlie/4463280095">z Q/flickr</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines. </p>

<p>Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.</p>

<p><iframe id="taviP" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/taviP/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A bar chart shows that 30% of faculty and staff had been bullied by students"></iframe></p>

<h2>What still isn’t known</h2>

<p>Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.</p>

<p>Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.</p>

<p>Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities. </p>

<p>Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture. </p>

<p>Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts. </p>

<p>Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.</p>

body: Some students can be aggressive if they don't like their grade. skynesher/E+ via Getty Images Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades , according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo
David Mulder/flickr , CC BY Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm
In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK
Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers
Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently
Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades
Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that
Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more
More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services , according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice
Why it matters Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions
Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade
Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation
Women and minority faculty are particularly affected
Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone
Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity
These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences
How we did our work We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K
Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors
A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades
A person sits in a chair facing an empty lecture hall. z Q/flickr , CC BY The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats
They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines
Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions
One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs
Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities
So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture
Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts
The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real
Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules

<title>US wildfire damage is on pace to triple by mid-century, but there are affordable ways to lower the risk</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768948/original/file-20261028-52-g8ffqc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C20%2C5808%2C3872&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A fast-moving fire burned hundreds of homes in Spokane, Wash., in August 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-embrace-while-searching-for-items-in-the-remains-of-news-photo/2289539473?phrase=wildfire%20damage&amp;adppopup=true">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78904-z">triple by mid-century</a>, my colleagues and I found in a study just published.</p>

<p>The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire <a href="https://doi.org/10.25810/9vsh-pb94">don’t have to be overly expensive</a>.</p>

<h2>The 2026 western fire season</h2>

<p>The 2026 wildfire season began with <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-historic-snow-drought-brings-worries-about-water-wildfires-and-the-future-in-the-west-279163">historically low mountain snowpack</a>, early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202608">hottest summer on record</a> intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.</p>

<p>Colorado’s <a href="https://wp-cpr.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2026/10/DFPC260781-Aspen-Acres-Signed-Final-Report-Compressed_Redacted.pdf">Aspen Acres Fire</a> destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving <a href="https://lessons.wildfire.gov/incident/knowles-fire-entrapment-2026">Knowles Fire overtook them</a> near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-spokane-wildfires-became-so-catastrophic-288895">Spokane, Washington</a>, damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People look out over a field toward a fire" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768949/original/file-20261028-52-p2jvo4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People watch from a police checkpoint as the Aspen Acres fire burns on July 1, 2026, near Pueblo, Colo. State investigators determined that a tree had fallen on a power line, starting the fire that grew to over 100,000 acres and burned more than 300 homes.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-watch-from-a-police-check-point-as-the-aspen-acres-news-photo/2283695651?phrase=colorado%20wildfire&amp;adppopup=true">Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In Colorado, the summer <a href="https://www.rmpbs.org/news/science-environment/strong-monsoon-season-outcome">monsoon season</a> brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.</p>

<p>Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had <a href="https://wildfiretrackers.com/f/united-states/colorado/wildfires">burned more than 318,000 acres</a> by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also <a href="https://www.nifc.gov/fire-information/nfn">well above average</a>. The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at <a href="https://www.nifc.gov/fire-information">Preparedness Level 5</a> – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a <a href="https://www.facebook.com/USForestService/posts/the-national-multiagency-coordination-group-sets-national-preparedness-levels-to/1371392061775752/">10-year average of 25 days</a> annually.</p>



<h2>Reasons for rising fire risk</h2>

<p>Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-america-courted-increasingly-destructive-wildfires-and-what-that-means-for-protecting-homes-today-247413">century of fire suppression</a> has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-matters/2025-in-review-us-temperatures">Rising temperatures</a> caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1607171113">nearly doubled the area burned</a> in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.</p>

<p>More people also now <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-fastest-population-growth-in-the-wests-wildland-urban-interface-is-in-areas-most-vulnerable-to-wildfires-173410">live in and at the edges of wildland areas</a>, raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.</p>

<p><iframe id="UbwNX" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/UbwNX/6/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Wildfire acreage by year"></iframe></p>

<p>These interacting factors have helped <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abc0020">nearly quadruple the annual area burned</a> in the western United States since 2000.</p>

<p>They also contribute to the growing threat of <a href="https://theconversation.com/la-fires-why-fast-moving-wildfires-and-those-started-by-human-activities-are-more-destructive-and-harder-to-contain-247314">fast-growing fires</a>, which can overwhelm emergency response. </p>

<p>In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adk5737">78% of documented structures destroyed</a> and 61% of reported firefighting costs.</p>

<p>A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.</p>

<h2>More homes in harm’s way</h2>

<p>The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage. </p>

<p>Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2020EF001795">expanded tenfold</a>, increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.</p>

<p>My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78904-z">up to 449,000 structures lost</a> between 2026 and 2060.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/AYvwogREEk4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How some basic steps to create defensible space can help make a home less likely to catch fire.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.</p>

<p>We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78904-z">greatest future risk are low-income communities</a>. In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire. </p>

<h2>How to lower your wildfire risk</h2>

<p>These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.</p>

<p>For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with <a href="https://firesafemarin.org/harden-your-home/fire-resistant-roofs/">Class A fire-resistant roofs</a> and <a href="https://firesafemarin.org/harden-your-home/fire-resistant-vents/">ember-resistant vents</a> that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. <a href="https://www.fire.ca.gov/dspace">Removing flammable debris</a>, mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. <a href="https://fireadaptedco.org/network-category/wildfire-councils/">Community programs</a> are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.</p>

<p>Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the <a href="https://dfpc.colorado.gov/colorado-wildfire-resiliency-code">Colorado fire code</a> increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lZ3ZQeC7VZQ?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">What home-hardening looks like.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it. </p>

<p>Beyond individual buildings, <a href="https://theconversation.com/wildfire-strategy-doesnt-need-a-winner-with-3-camps-fighting-for-dominance-the-system-cant-keep-up-with-the-risk-291343">prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning</a> operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and <a href="https://theconversation.com/electric-companies-dont-need-to-black-out-customers-to-prevent-wildfires-here-are-3-relatively-fast-affordable-solutions-285229">reduce the probability of ignition</a> while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can <a href="https://www.iawfonline.org/article/the-power-of-insurance-incentives-to-promote-fire-adapted-communities/">reward measurable risk reduction</a> and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.</p>

<p>These measures work best when they <a href="https://theconversation.com/wildfire-strategy-doesnt-need-a-winner-with-3-camps-fighting-for-dominance-the-system-cant-keep-up-with-the-risk-291343">reinforce one another</a>. The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287940/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Virginia Iglesias receives funding from the National Science Foundation and from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety</span></em></p></content>

title: What a blue wave could actually do

body: People line up to cast their ballots at a polling location in Charlotte, North Carolina, on November 3, 2026. | A.M
Stewart/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
This was already a record-breaking election, even before the polls opened today.  Campaigns and their allies poured record sums into political advertising
A near-record number of lawmakers are retiring or running for a different office, creating an unusually high number of open seats

And President Donald Trump’s approval ratings are approaching record lows, giving Democrats a rare opportunity: the chance to retake control of both chambers of Congress by cutting through some traditionally Republican states .  Both parties are framing the election in existential terms
Democrats have cast the midterms as an emergency brake on Trump and his agenda
And Republicans have characterized the election as a sort of firewall against far-left activists
Unsurprisingly, given those stakes, turnout has been historic

More than 59 million Americans voted early this year, which — you guessed it! — completely blew past the midterm early-vote record set by the 2022 elections.  In-person turnout looked similarly brisk in many places Tuesday, including Georgia , Florida and Maine
But it could be days or even weeks before we have full results, especially in very close races
And it will take much longer to figure out what those results mean for the rest of us
Go a little deeper View Link Democrats are really jazzed — almost queasily so — by the hope that they could retake Congress

Polls have consistently favored their candidates in the House, and they need to pick up four new seats to take control of the Senate.  Even if that happens, however, there are limits to what even a very large “blue wave” can achieve

Voters who expect their new lawmakers to ride into DC on white stallions and raze Trump’s agenda might find the next two years…a bit disappointing.  How disappointing? Well: My colleague Andrew Prokop recently asked congressional aides and outside experts what a Democratic majority could do over the rest of Trump’s second term
They “painted a picture of a grim slog akin to trench warfare.” Oof
Much of that prediction is simple mathematics
Most legislation requires 60 Senate votes to overcome a filibuster

And even the most optimistic predictions put Democrats short of that 60-vote threshold, which means that most bills they want to pass will need to attract (via compromise or political strong-arming) some number of Republican senators.  Contrary to my recollections of Schoolhouse Rock! , however, Congress’s powers don’t begin and end with the passing of bills
A majority in either chamber would give Democrats more leverage over congressional investigations and the ability to issue subpoenas

And if Dems win the Senate, they’d gain control over the confirmation process for senior administration officials and federal judges.  Subpoena power could allow for more robust investigations into things like the Trump family’s crypto investments and Trump’s fundraising for the White House ballroom

That Senate majority, meanwhile, would let Democrats block Trump’s nominees for judgeships and administration posts — a tantalizing prospect, since lower courts are growing alarmingly partisan and two of the conservatives on the Supreme Court are approaching 80 years old.   On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters that he would not expect a Democratic victory to persuade Trump to “change his ways.” “But we’re going to fight Trump tooth and nail…no matter what he does,” Schumer said
One link for later ➨ Take a moment to yourself
Today seems like as good a day as any to embrace the calming art of meditation! Set three minutes aside, find a quiet room, and focus on your breath
If you need a little more guidance, try a tool like Calm , Ten Percent Happier , Headspace , or the UCLA Mindful app
