title: Your guide to coping with election anxiety
excerpt: If you’re dealing with election-related stress, you’re not alone
body: If you’re dealing with election-related stress, you’re not alone
Editor’s note, November 3, 2026, 3 pm ET: This article was originally published in 2024 and has been updated for the 2026 midterm elections

If you’re heading to the polls today, you may be among the 30 percent of American voters who say the country’s political situation is the biggest source of stress in their lives right now, according to one poll

This unease makes sense, given how high the stakes are: Americans are voting for representatives who will make decisions about affordability , healthcare , and holding President Donald Trump to account
Elections are common wellsprings of anxiety because they’re rife with uncertainty, says David H
Rosmarin , the founder of the Center for Anxiety
You’re unsure of the outcome, and unsure of what life may look like for you under a new administration, especially when the difference between the two choices is undeniably vast
Some of the proposed policies may threaten people’s safety and freedoms, resulting in even more anxiety
Research shows political anxiety can impact people who aren’t generally anxious otherwise
There are key differences between everyday anxiety and election-related anxiety
Sometimes, generalized anxiety is rooted in cognitive distortions , or inaccurate beliefs or fears about the world

But election-based distress isn’t necessarily based on hypotheticals or overreactions, says licensed clinical social worker Jneé Hill . “A lot of the concerns,” she says, “are very real and very valid based on people’s real lives and lived experiences.” While election anxiety may feel large and existential, mental health experts agree it can be managed
As you wait for results to roll in, here are some strategies that can help quiet your mind
Get to the root of your anxiety To properly address your fears, you first need to specify what triggers your feelings of anxiety beyond not wanting the other side to win, Rosmarin says
What specific policies or issues impact you the most? It might be reproductive rights, the economy, immigration, or war abroad

Identify your top three issues, Rosmarin says, and try to share these worries with family, a friend, a supportive online community, or mental health professional.  Knowing the causes of your fears can help you anticipate and gird against them

Research shows when people were asked whether they expected to be stressed about the election the following day, they reported worse moods and were more likely to rate their physical health as poor, regardless of political affiliation, age, or gender.  Knowing the causes of your fears can help you anticipate and gird against them
You might also ask yourself why these issues concern you, Hill says

If reproductive rights are your top priority, maybe your deeper fears center on being unable to receive lifesaving medical treatments. “A lot of this,” Hill says, “comes down to safety.”  However, you can anticipate your stress and get in front of it

There’s a thought exercise you can do ahead of encountering something upsetting to slow your thoughts and talk yourself through your anxiety, says Shevaun Neupert , a psychology professor at North Carolina State University and author of a study on how to combat anticipatory election stress

Take a few minutes and think about why you’re stressed, how it’s related to the election, and why this contentious issue exists in the first place. “It really is focused on mental engagement, perspective-taking,” Neupert says, “trying to understand where did this thing come from? Why is it here? And to fully understand it rather than trying to solve it.” This exercise is effective, Neupert believes, because it helps reduce uncertainty
For instance, you may come to realize a source of your anxiety is a decades-long ongoing foreign policy issue

While this realization doesn’t minimize the problem or provide a solution, sometimes it’s helpful to put the issue into its proper context and perspective. “If we feel like we have a better understanding of a problem or of a stressor or we have a clearer sense of it,” Neupert says, “it’s not as scary.” Take control where you can Uncertainty about the future is a major source of general anxiety and can lead to a sense of powerlessness
With so much out of an individual’s control, it’s important to focus on areas where you do have authority

You can, of course, vote, volunteer as a poll worker, and get involved with get out the vote or activist organizations in your community.  You can also try setting goals in your work or social life that have nothing to do with politics but still might help you feel like you’re making progress in some small way, Neupert says
Maybe that goal is to finish a book over the next two weeks or to make dinner every night with your family. “That goes a long way to boosting perceptions of control,” she says
Then, consider how you’ll assert autonomy over your life after the election, especially if your candidate doesn’t win

You can plan on leaning heavily on your friends or distracting yourself with hobbies. “There might be situations that are beyond my control,” Rosmarin says, “but that doesn’t take away my power of choice in my life, in my limited way.” Lean into community Feeling supported by friends and family helps combat anxiety , so try to avoid spending the next few weeks in isolation
Instead, reach out to friends and family (preferably discussing anything but politics) or attend a safe and affirming community event

Find people who fill you with calm instead of dread and with whom you can talk things through and problem-solve. “What can be helpful,” clinical psychologist Krystal Lewis says, “is feeling all emotions, feeling all the feels, with people who are going through it as well.”  These communities will be especially crucial post-election, too, Lewis says
Find people or groups where you can process strong emotions, whether that’s a dance class or a volunteer organization

Care for your mind and body In the days leading up to the election and immediately following, especially if a clear winner is not apparent, stressed-out Americans should pay extra care to their minds and bodies
This might mean curbing your consumption of news and social media
While experts say everyone’s tolerance will be different, it’s important to pay attention to how they feel while watching or reading the news and social media

Engage enough to stay informed, but step away if you feel overwhelmed, Lewis says. “Unless that’s your job,” she says, “there’s no need to be that consumed with it.” Rosmarin suggests turning off your phone and avoiding all news at least 30 minutes before you go to sleep, including on election night. “You’ll wake up in the morning, you’ll find out what the story is

You watching it isn’t going to change anything,” he says. “The only thing it’ll change is make you more tired and grumpy the next day.” Engage enough to stay informed, but step away if you feel overwhelmed
Proper sleep, a healthy diet, and physical activity can ward off anxiety, so experts recommend getting enough to eat, moving a bit, and prioritizing rest
Try going for a walk or hike as exposure to nature can lower stress and anxiety levels
Grounding exercises can also help you calm down
Hill suggests deep breathing from your diaphragm or picking a color and describing objects of that color in your surroundings

title: Trump just said he was ending aid to Israel. He might actually mean it.
excerpt: An aerial view shows a campaign billboard depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 26, 2026, on th
body: An aerial view shows a campaign billboard depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 26, 2026, on the eve of the Israel's legislative elections. | Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the US would soon cut off military aid to Israel

During an Election Day interview with Fox & Friends , Trump said of Israel, “We were giving them $4 billion but it’s cut off at the end of the year.” When asked to explain this position, Trump said that Israel was a “very successful country” that didn’t need Americans’ money — and that the aid had become an “easy target” for “lunatics like [Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul] El-Sayed” in the midterm elections
Trump also suggested that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed with this reasoning and supported a cessation of US aid to his country
If all of his policy declarations could be taken at face value, then US soldiers would now be patrolling the streets of Gaza , while American hoteliers redeveloped its coastline
Further, Trump’s remarks Tuesday morning seem to have been ad-libbed
The Israeli Treasury Department reportedly had no knowledge of a supposed joint agreement to end US aid
And existing US law provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual funding through 2028
All this said, Trump didn’t pluck his Election Day rant out of thin air
Rather, his remarks actually reflect a prominent strain of thinking among Israeli leaders and security experts
In their view, America’s cash may no longer be worth the political blowback that it invites

Given this Israeli sentiment — and the souring of American public opinion toward Israel — the United States might very well draw down aid in the near future (although, probably not as soon as “the end of the year”)

The Israeli case against US aid to Israel During a May interview with 60 Minutes , Netanyahu said he would like to “draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have.” Amit Halevi, a lawmaker in Israel’s parliament and member of Netanyahu’s party, spelled out the logic of his position last year

In a pamphlet outlining his vision for the US-Israel relationship, Halevi said US military aid “creates a false narrative of dependency, weakens Israel’s global standing and subjects it to political pressure.” Halevi met with the leadership of the Heritage Foundation — arguably, the GOP’s most influential think tank — in 2025, shortly after Heritage had released its own controversial call for the ( very gradual) phasing out of US aid to Israel
Many on the Israeli right believe that such aid compromises Israeli sovereignty
As the retired Israel Defense Forces general Amir Avivi told Breitbart in 2024, aid “puts on Israel lots of restrictions,” which prevent it from pursuing its security interests with a free hand
Similar concerns have been voiced by former Israeli Prime Minster Naftali Bennet and ex-Israeli ambassador to Israel Michael Oren
Their argument boils down to two observations: There are many forms of US support that Israel would struggle to do without — but financial aid is not one of them
Direct financial aid provokes political blowback in a way that other, more essential forms of US assistance do not
In 2025, Israel spent about 7.9 percent of its GDP on the IDF
To sustain its 2025 level of military funding — without American cash — Israel would need to dedicate 8.5 percent of GDP to its military
But it would scarcely threaten Israel’s ability to pursue whatever foreign policy it sees fit
By contrast, Israel does need access to American military hardware
It has the money to fund its own military
But to adequately provision it, Israel must be allowed to purchase American-made fighter jets, among myriad other forms of martial technology
And the Israelis would also have a tough time doing without its broad military, diplomatic, and intelligence alliance with the United States
That alliance has attracted some criticism on the American left and right this year — particularly, after the US partnered with Israel to launch a war against Iran
But Israel’s American critics seem to have found the aid issue uniquely politically potent
Which makes sense: A voter doesn’t need to have any strong opinion about the Israel-Palestine conflict to oppose sending billions of dollars to a wealthy foreign country

Unlike proposals for an arms embargo or sanctions , cutting off aid speaks directly to Americans’ material interests; that money could be going to US citizens but is flowing to the Israeli military instead

In his Senate race, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has tried to tap into this isolationist sentiment, describing his plans for slashing aid to Israel — and increasing benefits for US citizens — as an “ America First ” agenda

Meanwhile, in a controversial ad, an outside group supporting El-Sayed’s candidacy made this argument in blunter terms, portraying a couple forced to pare back their grocery list, in order to save enough money for “killing Palestinians.” New @RebellionPac ad dropping in Michigan
We have to suffer here at home, so Israel can get all its wars
That’s why they buy politicians like Mike Rogers

He promised to serve Israel “unconditionally,” but never made that promise to you. pic.twitter.com/mtgVOyNczg — Cenk Uygur (@cenkuygur) October 24, 2026 US aid to Israel is not actually responsible for Americans’ rising grocery bills (although, the war in Iran plausibly is)
But the broader isolationist argument has wide resonance
In a recent survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, a majority of Americans favored either reducing or ending aid to Israel
And whether or not Trump’s aid comments referred to a solid plan, his political aides swiftly used them to reclaim the “America First” banner from Democrats like El-Sayed

America First. pic.twitter.com/RyLif7XuB6 — Trump War Room (@TrumpWarRoom) November 3, 2026 Faced with these dynamics, it isn’t hard to see how an Israeli leader might think it best to beat a strategic retreat on financial aid.  A phase-out of US aid may be coming, whether Israel likes it or not To be clear, Israel’s leadership is by no means united in favor of Trump’s impromptu proposal
Indeed, even those who support winding down US aid have insisted that this withdrawal of financial backing must be gradual
And Gadi Eisenkot, the man most likely to become Israel’s next prime minister, is a staunch advocate for indefinite US aid

title: The Supreme Court sounds eager to make you pay for anti-LGBTQ schools
excerpt: Protesters for and against transgender athletes competing in women's sports gather outside the Supreme Court on January 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Heather D
body: Protesters for and against transgender athletes competing in women's sports gather outside the Supreme Court on January 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images There was one significant surprise during the Supreme Court’s Tuesday argument in St
Roy , a case asking whether Colorado may require schools that accept state funding to treat LGBTQ families and students the same way they treat anyone else
For a brief moment, Chief Justice John Roberts seemed like he might break with his Republican colleagues and uphold Colorado’s policy
Mary arises out of a program that provides state-funded preschool to all Colorado children
Families are allowed to choose which school they wish their young child to attend, and private religious schools are eligible to participate in this program
But state law also prohibits any school that receives this funding from discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity
The plaintiffs include Catholic-identified schools that wish to exclude the children of same-sex couples, but that claim they should nonetheless be funded by Colorado’s taxpayers
In recent years, the Court has followed a consistent pattern in cases that pit religious conservatives against LGBTQ Americans — religious conservatives always win
As several justices noted during Tuesday’s arguments, the Court’s legal doctrines governing these cases are incoherent and often seem to call for illogical results
When a religious conservative seeks an exemption from a state or federal law that prohibits anti-LGBTQ discrimination, this Court gives them the exemption
Mary argument, these plaintiffs are asking the Court to reach beyond its previous precedents
Makin (2022), the Court required Maine to include religious schools in a tuition voucher program that, under Maine law, only funded secular private schools
But Colorado’s program includes religious schools.  Colorado is perfectly willing to subsidize Catholic schools
It merely insists that those schools, like all other preschools in Colorado, must treat gay and trans people the same way they treat anyone else if they receive taxpayers’ money
If a Catholic school (or any other religious school, for that matter) does not wish to comply with this condition, it may still operate
It just won’t receive money from the state

Yet, while Roberts’s first questions during Tuesday’s argument suggested that he might consider voting in favor of Colorado, none of his five Republican colleagues appeared open to that position (although Justice Amy Coney Barrett did ask some questions suggesting that she may hand Colorado a narrower loss than the Court’s right flank would prefer)

And, by the end of the argument, even Roberts seemed sympathetic to the orthodox Republican position that, when LGBTQ rights conflict with religious conservatism, the religious party wins.  This suggests that soon, taxpayers will be required to fund discriminatory institutions, even in states where such discrimination is forbidden by law

The two partisan factions on the Supreme Court live in completely different universes in religion cases Roberts’s early question aside, one thing that was absolutely clear from Tuesday’s argument is that the Court’s Democratic minority and its Republican majority bring completely different values to the table in cases like St

All three of the Court’s Democrats expressed concern that, if their Court doesn’t someday draw a line in the sand and say that religious conservatives do not receive literally any accommodation that they ask for in federal litigation, then that will lead to immoral results and prevent important American institutions from functioning

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, asked why, if religious schools are permitted to discriminate against gay people, aren’t they also allowed to discriminate against Black people? What if, for example, someone who sincerely believes that racial segregation is mandated by God opens up a school that excludes Black children? Similarly, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson asked about a hypothetical school which teaches that only boys, and not girls, should be taught mathematics

Mary , why wouldn’t this school be entitled to an exemption from state laws requiring all schools to teach certain subjects, including math, to all students? Meanwhile, Justice Elena Kagan asked deputy US solicitor general Sarah Harris (the Trump administration, naturally, supports the anti-LGBTQ side in St
Mary ) whether ordinary public schools would be subject to a rule requiring states to accommodate the religious beliefs of anti-LGBTQ parents

When Harris indicated that they would, Kagan then asked why the parent of a public school student couldn’t demand that their child be educated in a different classroom than the children of same-sex parents — or demand some other accommodation that public schools would find it very difficult to provide? But the Republican justices dismissed these concerns, with many of them suggesting that religious objectors may demand an exemption from nearly any law

The dominant view among the Court’s Republicans appeared to be that any law that imposes obligations on a religious conservative must survive a rigid legal rule known as “ strict scrutiny ,” the most skeptical level of review that courts apply in constitutional cases
Nearly all government policies that are subjected to strict scrutiny fail, so, if strict scrutiny applies in cases like St
Mary , that would mean that religious conservatives nearly always prevail
Though, in fairness, Eric Rassbach, the plaintiffs’ lawyer in St
Mary , did suggest that a ban on race discrimination might be the rare law that can be enforced against religious schools
So, under the Republican justices’ approach, religious schools may not be allowed to exclude Black students
But they’d have free rein to violate many other laws
With the exception of Roberts, the only Republican on the Court who seemed open to a more nuanced rule than simply applying strict scrutiny in every case was Barrett
And it’s not like Barrett was particularly sympathetic to the state
Still, Barrett did float a way to decide this case that may be slightly narrower than many of her Republican colleagues’ views

Briefly, Barrett drew a distinction between a school that outright forbids the children of same-sex parents from attending, and a school that allows these children to attend, but only if the parents sign a statement denouncing homosexuality and agreeing to restrictions on their personal conduct — such as never appearing together at the school at the same time, so that no one can see that one of the school’s students has two parents of the same sex

Barrett seemed to suggest that perhaps the Court could uphold Colorado’s ban on absolute exclusion, while simultaneously permitting religious schools to impose these humiliating obligations on same-sex families

As a practical matter, however, it is unclear how this rule would differ from one endorsing total exclusion of gay parents, because what parent would agree to these restrictions? In any event, after Tuesday’s argument, it is hard to imagine the Court handing Colorado, or same-sex parents, anything that resembles a real win
Whether the Court endorses allowing schools to exclude same-sex parents entirely, or embraces something like Barrett’s rule, the practical result is likely to be the same
Religious conservatives get what they want; LGBTQ Americans must yield to the interests of those conservatives.

title: Israel’s Arab parties could end Netanyahu’s rule — if his opposition lets them
excerpt: Israeli left-wing activists hold placards and chant slogans during a demonstration calling for a formation of a government together with Arab parties in Tel Avi
body: Israeli left-wing activists hold placards and chant slogans during a demonstration calling for a formation of a government together with Arab parties in Tel Aviv on October 28, 2026, a day after Israel's legislative elections. | Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images The dust is beginning to settle a week after Israel’s first national election since Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023 , and the war Israel waged on Gaza in response
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his opponents won the 61 parliamentary seats needed to govern

Now the fate of the next government hinges on a less-discussed part of the Israeli electorate: Arab citizens , who voted in record numbers and whose parties have emerged with more leverage than ever before
They are not to be confused with the roughly 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who live under Israeli control but are not citizens and cannot vote in national elections

Although Israel has become a fault line in both American parties, with Democrats split over arms sales and whether to call the war in Gaza a genocide , and Republicans over whether Israel pulled the United States into war with Iran, these were not the central issues in the recent election
Voters and candidates alike treated the election as a referendum on Netanyahu himself, who has governed Israel for most of the past 17 years and is currently on trial for corruption

And Netanyahu did lose support in this election: His right-wing and religious coalition fell from 64 of the Knesset’s 120 seats in 2022 to 53, while 67 seats went to parties that ran against him.  Nineteen of those 67 opposition seats were won by two Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, on a historic surge in turnout among Arab citizens of Israel
Arab parties had held just 10 seats after the last election
Key takeaways Israel’s election ended in deadlock, and record Arab turnout nearly doubled Arab parties’ seats to 19, the most ever
A crime wave in Arab towns while Netanyahu’s far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir ran the police drove Arab voters to the polls
Depending on the details, a Jewish-Arab coalition could reshape Israeli politics, but it won’t end the occupation or reverse course in Gaza
But most of Israel’s Jewish parties have long treated a governing coalition that depends on Arab votes as taboo
Netanyahu spent the campaign portraying Ra’am and Joint List politicians as supporters of terrorism , and several of his Jewish opponents promised to never govern with them

Whether the four Jewish-led opposition parties that call themselves the “change bloc” will break that promise is now the central political question hanging over Israel — with major implications for Arab and Jewish citizens alike, and for what kind of country they share. “There’s been a fair amount of commentary from American Jewish groups that over a million Arab citizens can vote, and that’s true, but the big asterisk is it matters only if those votes are taken seriously and if Arabs are treated as potential partners in a coalition,” Ilan Goldenberg, the chief policy officer for J Street, a liberal pro-Israel group founded as a counterweight to AIPAC, told me. “Otherwise it’s a pretty empty symbol, and it says something else about Israeli society and Israeli politics.” Polling suggests most change bloc voters would accept a government that relied on Ra’am, if not the Joint List, whether inside the coalition or backing it from outside in exchange for policy commitments
Their leaders have been more cautious, though, partly because most Jewish Israelis still oppose an Arab-Jewish coalition and the politicians worry about losing those voters in the next election

Critics see that caution as the problem: Rather than try to bring the Israeli public along, the Jewish opposition leaders campaigned on rejecting an alliance they might need to form any kind of government at all

It’s a pivotal moment for supporters of a liberal, democratic Israel, for those pushing sanctions and boycotts — some of whom want an end to Israel as a Jewish state — and for the roughly 900,000 Arab citizens who turned out to vote for urgent improvements in their daily lives

The next few months will decide who governs the country, whether Arab voters get real influence over policy or become further marginalized, whether pressure on Israel from abroad grows or fades, and whether anything changes for the Palestinians it rules
Why Arab voters showed up For Arab voters, this election was different in two ways
The Arab parties were more united than ever on a single priority — getting rid of Netanyahu — even if it meant working with Zionist parties whose vision of a Jewish state they’ve long opposed

And calls to boycott the vote, which Islamist and Palestinian nationalist groups within Israel’s Arab community have pushed in past elections on the grounds that voting legitimizes the state, were far more muted this time around.  The prime motivating factor for Arab voters was Netanyahu’s coalition itself, the most right-wing government in Israel’s history

Its national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was once convicted of inciting racism after displaying a sign reading “Expel the Arab enemy,” has overseen the police while organized crime has killed record numbers of Arab citizens
Homicides in Arab communities more than doubled between 2022 and 2025, and police solved just 12 percent of them in the first half of this year

Netanyahu’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who has said there is “no such thing as a Palestinian people,” also froze hundreds of millions of shekels promised to Arab towns, arguing the money would reach criminals

In 2025, Britain and four other countries sanctioned both men for inciting violence against Palestinians. “The feeling is the state has completely failed to address criminal violence,” Yousef Munayyer, a Palestinian citizen of Israel and the head of the Palestine/Israel program at the Arab Center Washington DC , told me. “Brutal murders go uninvestigated and unsolved, and in many corners there’s a belief that the Israeli intelligence services are intentionally turning a blind eye.”  Hassan Jabareen, the executive director of Adalah , a legal advocacy group for Palestinian citizens of Israel, told me the Arab parties have been deliberately keeping their demands to things an anti-Netanyahu government could practically deliver, like fighting crime, ending the demolition of Bedouin homes in southern Israel, and stopping settler violence in the West Bank .  “We are not going to say to end the occupation, we are not going to ask for withdrawal from Syria,” Jabareen said. “Those issues, we know that they won’t agree with us, and the right-wing will use it against them, and they themselves won’t agree.” Though Ra’am and the Joint List did not make Gaza central to their campaigns, Jabareen said the national election was a rare opportunity for Arab voters to express their anger at the war, something they’ve been heavily barred from protesting over the last three years
He added that Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank have been “happy and proud” of the record turnout of Arab citizens
The choice facing Gadi Eisenkot The “change bloc” is an alliance of four Zionist parties with little in common beyond wanting Netanyahu gone
Its leader is Gadi Eisenkot , a former army chief who sat in Netanyahu’s war cabinet after October 7, lost a son in Gaza, and quit the government over its handling of the war
His new centrist party won the most seats of the four
The others are a party led by two former prime ministers, the settler-right hawk Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid, and Yair Golan’s party, the last of Israel’s Zionist left
The fourth is Avigdor Lieberman’s, hawkish on security and built on secular Russian-speaking immigrants who want the ultra-Orthodox out of government
The four were split on Arab parties during the campaign
Golan was the only leader explicitly open to governing with them

Eisenkot set four conditions for any coalition partner, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and Hamas as a terrorist group, and said in September that no Arab party met them. (Arab leaders and many critics saw these conditions as a way to shut Arabs out without saying so.) Bennett, who in 2021 led the first governing coalition ever to include an independent Arab party, said this time he wanted only Zionist parties in government, and Lieberman, who sat in that same 2021 coalition, also ruled out relying on Arab parties again

Ori Kol, a progressive campaigner who worked for Golan’s left-wing party, told me most Jewish opposition voters “were shocked” on election night, expecting the change bloc to win more seats. “What people really expected is that Netanyahu voters would not turn out as they did, because the logic was after three years of war, two failed wars against Iran, attacking Qatar, the sanctions, and the incredible physical, emotional and economic toll on the country every Israeli living here has experienced, that Netanyahu would pay some sort of cost,” he said
And while Netanyahu’s coalition did lose about a dozen seats compared to 2022, his party still did better than expected, beating the final polls from three major Israeli broadcasters
So what is the resistance to forming a Jewish-Arab government? Part of it is plain prejudice, a refusal to accept Arab parties as legitimate partners in governing a Jewish state
Arab parties have supported or joined an Israeli government only twice, briefly, in the 1990s and in 2021, and both times the Jewish parties involved treated it as a one-off they’d rather not repeat

Both times, too, the Arab parties were just a handful of votes at the margin, while this time they would represent nearly a third of the coalition.  A vocal liberal minority of Israelis say that’s exactly the change the country is overdue for
In the week since the election, thousands have rallied to demand their leaders form a Jewish-Arab government

title: What Democrats could actually do if they win Congress
excerpt: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) walks with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) in May 2026 in Washington, DC. | Win McNamee/Getty Images Th
body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) walks with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) in May 2026 in Washington, DC. | Win McNamee/Getty Images The outcome of the midterm elections is perhaps the single most important factor in determining how the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency will play out — and what impact it will have on people’s lives in the United States and around the world

If Republicans defy the polls and hold both chambers, Trump would have the chance to pass more sweeping legislation on party-line votes, confirm more loyalist nominees to important positions, and continue remaking the judiciary, all while keeping oversight to a minimum
Democrats would have limited tools to object, Republicans would keep a free hand to run Washington, and Trump would be able to cite the results to maintain party loyalty
Practically and politically, the next two years would look a lot like the last two

Conversely, the better Democrats do, the more power they will have to block Trump’s agenda, check his power, investigate his administration, and advance priorities of their own on issues like the economy, healthcare, the war in Iran, immigration enforcement, corruption, and more

But they’d also face significant limits on their power, from the Senate filibuster and Trump’s veto pen to White House tactics that could delay or derail oversight.  Key takeaways Even if Democrats romp in the congressional midterms this week, they won’t be able to do whatever they want; however, if they use their powers creatively, they could achieve real and meaningful accomplishments

Legislative accomplishments would likely happen in one of three ways: through confrontations on “must-pass” bills, through bipartisanship, or by laying the groundwork for bills a future Democratic president could sign

House or Senate majorities would give Democrats subpoena powers, but the Trump administration will likely refuse to comply; Democrats would have to think outside the box in how to make their investigations succeed
A Senate majority would make it far more challenging for Trump to confirm nominees and would slow his judicial confirmations to a trickle, if that

So what are the real midterm stakes? Which moves from a Democratic Congress would be symbolic and which could have an immediate impact on real-world outcomes? And what might prevent them from achieving their goals?   To get a better sense of what Democrats could actually do if they won power in Congress, I spoke to current and former congressional aides as well as plugged-in outside experts
They generally painted a picture of a grim slog akin to trench warfare
Some believed the expectations of the Democratic base would far outpace what could realistically be achieved, and that frustration and disappointment were inevitable

But some also expressed surprising optimism that, if Democrats played their cards right, they could score real and meaningful accomplishments — in driving policy change, in bringing wrongdoing to light, and in laying the groundwork for far more ambitious goals in the near future

Whether they can do this will depend in part on politics and messaging, but also on how they use the formal tools that would be newly available to them with a congressional takeover: legislation, investigations, and — in the case of a Senate win — the confirmation process

Legislation: How new Democratic majorities could legislate in a way that actually matters House Democratic leaders are proudly talking about the bills they plan to quickly pass if they win the majority on topics such as healthcare, tariffs, and the war in Iran

But the reality is that, so long as the Senate’s 60-vote requirement for ordinary legislation to advance remains in place, such bills aren’t going to make it to Trump’s desk without winning significant Republican support. (And even if they do make it to Trump’s desk — say, via the special budget reconciliation process — he could veto them.) Instead, for Democratic majorities to do meaningful things with legislation under Trump, they’d likely have to pursue one of the following three approaches. 1

Confrontations on the must-pass bills Lots of bills go nowhere in Congress, but some are viewed as “must-pass.” Some have practical consequences for failure after a certain deadline: If the debt ceiling isn’t raised, the country will default on its debt with potentially catastrophic consequences ; if government funding bills aren’t passed, the government will shut down, as it did for 43 days last year

Often, if one or both chambers flip in the midterms, a bold new majority tries to use one of these bills to make policy demands on the president, believing the bill’s “must-pass” status gives them leverage
Then, a showdown unfolds, as both sides play chicken before a looming deadline

So if Democrats win the majority, they will have to decide: Which much-pass bills do they want to make demands over, what do they want to demand, and just how hard do they want to demand it? Experts I spoke to were skeptical Democrats would push too hard on the debt ceiling. “The Democratic position in the past has been, ‘We don’t threaten the full faith and credit of the US government,’” Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, told me
The consequences of default seem, to them, too devastating to risk, and they’re historically reluctant to legitimize Republicans’ use of the debt ceiling as a weapon under Democratic presidents

Some sort of fight seems likelier on government funding — after all, even while in the Senate minority, Democrats used the filibuster to shut down the government late last year , demanding that Republicans extend subsidies for the Affordable Care Act

They could run that playbook again, saying they won’t fund the government unless Trump agrees to their demands on healthcare (such as rolling back Trump’s Medicaid cuts ), ICE (where they’ve demanded new accountability measures and restrictions ), or other issues.  Many are skeptical that Democrats will successfully strong-arm Trump into making concessions in this way

When last year’s shutdown stretched for over a month and its consequences — for unpaid government workers and recipients of government benefits — grew more acute, enough Democrats eventually gave in even as they seemed to have the upper hand in polling
But it’s likely that the party’s base will urge them to try again — and if they do, their theory that they have more leverage over Trump this time will be tested. 2

Bipartisanship The alternative to trying to shake the president down is to actually try and get Republican votes — passing measures with bipartisan support.  And don’t scoff — though partisan battles will get all the headlines, there’s still a surprising amount of bipartisan action on substantive issues in Congress
During the final two years of Trump’s first term, bipartisan bills on Covid relief , energy , and trade passed
Under President Joe Biden, bills on infrastructure , semiconductors , same-sex marriage , and presidential election reform won bipartisan support
And this year, a bipartisan housing bill became law, and Congress hopes to pass an electricity permitting reform deal before the end of the year, too
Some of these bills were standalone; others became law because they were attached to must-pass bills, such as government funding, or the National Defense Authorization Act

That’s a potential way to get something Trump doesn’t like into law — get enough Republicans on board, and hope that either Trump will conclude it’s too much of a headache to veto it, or that support in Congress is so strong his veto will fail (two-thirds of both the House and Senate can vote to override a veto)
There’s precedent from this year’s bipartisan housing bill, which Trump allowed to become law without his signature

Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told me that Democrats could try to add riders on appropriations bills that block certain controversial Trump administration regulatory actions. “That feels potentially achievable to me,” he said

But, to get those bills to Trump’s desk, they’d have to get the consent of Republican negotiators in Congress.  Bipartisanship can be achieved through working with the other party and compromising with them

But another route is through political pressure — say, if a proposal is so popular and politically potent that the other party feels they have no choice but to go along. “Bipartisanship is not always the signal of a kumbaya environment,” Charlie Ellsworth, a former aide to Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer who currently advises the advocacy group Public Citizen, told me.  That’s what happened with Rep
Ro Khanna’s (D-CA) bill to release the Epstein files last year; GOP leaders tried to hold it back, but the dam broke and it eventually passed with overwhelming majorities in both chambers
If Democrats win the majority, they could similarly put pressure on the GOP by forcing votes on issues where the party might be divided — like tariffs , or the Iran war . 3

Groundwork for the future   The other route for legislating to really matter in the next session is more forward-looking — Democrats could be crafting bills that they truly intend to pass in 2029, if a new Democratic president is sworn in and the party holds Congress
The idea here is that the next president may have a limited window to pass major legislation, so he or she will be looking for ideas to take off the shelf
And the more serious legislative work that gets done in this Congress, and the more Democratic consensus is built ahead of time, the better-prepared certain bills could be for that opportunity

title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
excerpt: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization
body: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization
Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights
But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired
Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement
And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics
Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage

This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business
Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver
On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business
That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago
But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses
Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage
At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average
In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business
The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall
The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights
Insufficient context reduces insight quality
When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives
Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%
Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context
Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness
At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon
Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive
Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights
The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%)
They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%)
The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents
Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff
It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
excerpt: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once
body: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once
It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors
A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt
The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes
With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive
The financial pressure is already visible
Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code
GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits
Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents
But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value
Cost per token measures consumption, not results
Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops
Some represents the work of shipping software
A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap
Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged
Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software
The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work
Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step
Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning
Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency
This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical
Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks
That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow
Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work
Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity
With rented inference, every call adds to the bill
With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more
Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered
The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code
When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise
Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls
That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting
Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI

title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves
But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality
They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts
This new era is being called the agentic web
It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess

Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide
They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults
Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits
But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign

Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter
Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. ( BBC ) + The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. ( NBC News ) + OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. ( CNBC ) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Hackers have hit Ukraine and Russia’s emergency alert apps Kyiv residents were warned of “nuclear danger.” ( NBC News ) + Russia’s app said nuclear warheads had been launched. ( CNN ) + Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. ( BI ) + AI will transform cyber warfare. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. ( Guardian ) + Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. ( Reuters $) + But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. ( Gizmodo ) 4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. ( Wired $) + We need real-time tracking of AI agents. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. ( Reuters $) + Virtual power plants could help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. ( Bloomberg $) + But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” ( 404 Media ) 7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. ( Politico ) 8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. ( WSJ $) 9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.( Gizmodo ) 10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. ( Quanta ) Quote of the day “It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.” —Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society

One more thing Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away
He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function
But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.  Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility
And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
excerpt: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since
body: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991
But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare)

body: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country

body: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths , Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies

body: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days
